title: Make the profile's paths repo-relative, so git and the downwind maps agree by construction
description:
git reports paths relative to the REPOSITORY ROOT, whatever directory the
command ran from. The profile stores paths relative to a root cli.py sets to
Path.cwd(). These coincide only when smoke-optimiser happens to be run from the
repository root, and differ permanently in a monorepo where the Python project
is one directory of a larger repo -- exactly the layout where selecting a subset
matters most.

The failure mode is silence. A changed path 'services/api/db/models.py' is
simply absent from a map keyed by 'db/models.py', so it matches nothing and the
selection returns no tests for a file plenty of tests depend on.

TWO ANCHORS, NAMED APART. The single `project_root` in the code today is doing
two jobs that only look like one because the guard forces them equal:

* REPO_ROOT -- `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`. The path space the profile's
  paths, git's output and the scope roots are all expressed in. Outside a git
  repository it falls back to the invocation directory, which is sound because
  downwind selection is unavailable there anyway -- there is no diff to select
  from -- while profiling and the coverage-per-second mode keep working.
* INVOCATION_DIR -- the cwd. Where `[tool.smoke_optimiser]` and
  `[tool.coverage.run]` are read from, where `profile_path` and
  `downwind_file_path` resolve against, and the cwd the pytest subprocess is
  given.

So the consuming repo is run from its project directory (`cd api && smoke-
optimiser downwind`), and the tool stops requiring that directory to be the
repository root. pytest therefore sees the pyproject.toml that configures it,
which is the whole reason the invocation directory cannot simply be moved: a
project's `testpaths`, `pythonpath` and `asyncio_mode` are all rootdir-relative
and none of them are visible from the repository root.

Everything below the CLI is already parameterised for this and already handles
the split: coverage_db.py:295 relativises absolute coverage paths in the parent,
import_tracer.py:209 and read_tracer.py:172 do the same for the graph and the
read map, scope.py:142-172 resolves cov sources and test paths against
invocation_dir before relativising to the repo root, and every function in
downwind/changes.py already takes repo_root as a parameter. runner.py:694 says
outright that pytest's rootdir is not obliged to match. What this issue changes
is the two roots being told apart at the top, and the three places that
entangled them.

NODE IDS ARE THE FIRST ENTANGLEMENT, and the reason this is not simply "stop
calling Path.cwd()". Node ids are relative to pytest's ROOTDIR, and maps.py:96-
113 folds `_defining_file(test_id)` straight into known_files alongside
repo-relative coverage paths. Once the two roots differ, known_files holds two
path spaces at once -- 'api/auth.py' beside 'tests/test_auth.py' -- so
`maps.knows()` answers False for every changed test file and the selection
refuses to the full suite on most commits. Safe, but useless, and it presents as
"downwind never selects anything" rather than as an error.

The fix is a recorded NODE_ID_PREFIX: pytest's rootdir relative to the repo
root, read inside the profiled process where rootdir is known, and applied only
where `_defining_file` derives a path -- `_known_files`,
`_tests_in_module_by_file` and `tests_at_or_below`. Map KEYS become
repo-relative; the node ids those maps hold as VALUES are stored and returned
exactly as pytest reported them. Nothing is ever stripped: the selection returns
raw node ids, .downwind.json carries them raw, plugin.py:189 keeps matching
`item.nodeid` verbatim and needs no change, and `.smoke_suite.json`'s test_ids
stay feedable to `--smoke` for free.

The precision trap: the prefix is `config.rootpath`, NOT
`config.invocation_params.dir`. Node ids are rootdir-relative, while
`resolve_scope`'s existing use of invocation_dir for positional args is correct
because args are cwd-relative. The two coincide today and would drift apart the
moment this lands.

THE PROFILE RECORDS WHERE IT WAS TAKEN FROM, as the invocation directory's
offset from the repo root, alongside the node-id prefix -- relative, never
absolute. Without it a profile captured under the old convention, or from a
different subdirectory, matches nothing and reports a healthy-looking zero. A
relative offset catches exactly that while staying checkout-independent, so a
profile copied into a fresh git worktree keeps working and so-c76.4's question
about sharing one across worktrees stays open to be decided on its merits. An
absolute path would close it by making it an error.

A profile whose offset disagrees with the run's is OUTDATED, not MISCONFIGURED:
regenerating is the entire fix, so the ordinary fallback repairs it.

ARTEFACT PATHS ARE THE THIRD ENTANGLEMENT, and one of them is a live bug the
moment the roots differ. `profile_path` and `downwind_file_path` resolve against
the INVOCATION DIR in all three places that currently disagree -- cli.py:260
joins them onto the root, downwind uses them bare, and
`_drop_own_artefacts` joins them onto repo_root. That last one compares its
resolved paths against `changed`, whose paths are repo-relative from git: anchor
the artefacts on the repo root while they actually live in api/ and the
comparison never matches, so the profile the run just rewrote reads as a
working-tree change on the next run, every run refuses, and every refusal
rewrites the profile again. A permanent full suite that looks like ordinary
operation.

Where the artefacts were written is NOT separately recorded. Under this rule
they live in the invocation directory by definition, so the offset above already
says where they were, and a second copy could only ever disagree with the first.

NO BACK-COMPAT SHIM IS NEEDED. PROFILE_SCHEMA_VERSION (models.py:11) already
fails a mismatched profile with a regenerate path, and the downwind fallback
then rebuilds it, so bumping the version is self-healing.

config.py (its `project_root` parameter is the invocation dir), downwind/
command.py (`_resolve_repo_root` relaxes from "invocation dir EQUALS repo root"
to "is INSIDE the repo", `_report_wrong_directory` goes, `_run_pytest` runs
pytest in the invocation dir rather than the repo root, `_drop_own_artefacts`
re-anchors, and the module docstring's refusal paragraph is rewritten),
downwind/maps.py (`_defining_file` and its three callers), profiler/runner.py
(the hook reports the node-id prefix beside the scope it already writes; the
subprocess cwd and PYTHONPATH become the invocation dir; SMOKE_PROJECT_ROOT is
renamed to say which root it means), profiler/scope.py, coverage_db.py,
import_tracer.py and read_tracer.py (their `project_root` parameters already
mean the repo root and should say so), and the profile schema.

persistence.py's no-scope message currently advises "Profile from the repository
root, not from a subdirectory", which this change makes wrong.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, do not re-propose:

- Keeping cwd-relative paths and translating git's output at the point of use.
  Smaller change, but every future consumer of git output has to remember the
  translation, and forgetting it under-selects silently rather than failing.
- Relying on the full-suite fallback to cover the mismatch. It does fail safe
  today, since every changed file looks new -- but only until something optimises
  that fallback away, and a systematic mismatch that looks like healthy operation
  is exactly what this design refuses to rely on.
- A --project-root flag letting the user declare the root. Rejected: the tool
  already shells out to git and can discover the root itself, and a flag is a
  manual step that can be set wrong.
- Asking the consuming repo to move its pyproject.toml to the git root instead.
  This was the first plan for casey_ai and it is the wrong way round -- the repo
  would be changing shape to satisfy a constraint the tool does not actually
  have.
- Keeping the invocation at the repo root and discovering the project directory
  by searching for a pyproject.toml. With no pyproject at the root there is
  nowhere to declare where the project is, so the rule would have to be invented,
  and a wrong guess picks the wrong pytest configuration silently.
- Rewriting node ids into repo-relative space in the profile and stripping the
  prefix back off wherever one is handed to pytest. More self-consistent on disk,
  but every consumer of a node id -- .downwind.json, .smoke_suite.json, the report
  header, the not-found warnings -- becomes a place the strip can be forgotten.

  it finds, and none of those are visible from the root. The alternative --
  discovering the project directory by searching from the root -- was rejected
  because with no pyproject at the root there is nowhere to declare where the
  project is, so the rule would have to be invented.
- Node ids are stored VERBATIM and only the derived map keys are normalised. The
  original body said both this and "strip the prefix again when writing
  .downwind.json", which are different designs; storing them verbatim means
  nothing has to remember to strip.
- The recorded root is a RELATIVE offset, not an absolute path. An absolute one
  would have made sharing a profile across worktrees of the same repository an
  error, closing so-c76.4's open question by accident.
- The artefacts are anchored on the invocation directory and the profile does NOT
  separately record where they were written: under that rule they live there by
  definition, so the offset already says it.

Two things surfaced that the body had not anticipated. The anchor mismatch needed
its own ProfileFault -- reported as OUTDATED it came out in the schema
mismatch's words, telling the user their profile was from a different build of
the tool when it was from a different directory. And the artefact anchoring was
a live bug rather than a tidy-up: _drop_own_artefacts compared repo-root-anchored
artefact paths against git's repo-relative output, so in a subdirectory the
profile the tool had just rewritten read as an unattributable change, every run
refused, and every refusal rewrote it again. There is now a test that fails
against the old anchoring.

Verified against the real consumer's layout: casey_ai/api resolves to
repo_root=/Users/mikel/code/casey_ai, project_offset=api, cov_source=. from
[tool.coverage.run], coverage root api. Its suite was not run -- that is
agent_rules ar-gcw.4.

Left over: so-u3z, the unbounded-test-scope warning going quiet for a
subdirectory project, which this change causes and does not fix.

title: Capture the real import graph during profiling, so a change to an import-only module selects its importers instead of the whole suite
description:
so-d8v gave the profile per-test files_covered and top-level measured_files. That fixes the REASONING for a changed file no test executes at runtime, but not the SELECTION: a Pydantic model or constants module that only ever runs at import time still forces a full-suite run, because coverage records import-time execution under the empty context and never records WHO imported it.

The missing relation is the import graph. With it, a changed import-only module selects the tests whose modules transitively import it, which measurement shows is a 60-83% saving over running everything (see NOTES).

Scope of this issue is CAPTURE ONLY -- record the graph into the profile. Consuming it for selection is so-jr5.
acceptance_criteria: A profile recorded from a suite where module A imports module B, and module C also imports B with A collected first, contains BOTH the A->B and C->B edges. A module imported only at collection time (never executed under any test context) still has its importers recorded. Edges resolve to project-relative file paths; site-packages and .venv are excluded.
notes:
MEASUREMENT THAT JUSTIFIES THIS (2026-09-06). Percentage of the suite an import
closure selects, computed per source file, via a --collect-only prototype:

repo                tests  files   p25    median   p75    max     mean
smoke-optimiser        81     19  18.5%   27.2%   48.1%  87.7%   33.3%
casey_ai/api         1389    143  20.5%   47.7%   52.1%  96.5%   39.4%
enphase_curtailer    2600    271   7.3%   12.8%   21.9%  93.2%   17.5%

Against the current 100% fallback that is a 60-83% saving on exactly the edits
that trigger a full run today.

The decisive case is casey_ai: db/models/common.py reaches 96.5% of the suite
(genuinely global, running everything IS right), while db/models/interval.py and
db/models/task.py reach 3 tests each (0.2%) -- same directory, same kind of
declaration file, not re-exported through the package __init__. Today all three
are treated identically. The graph gets both right.

CAVEAT ON THE NUMBERS: measured with --collect-only, which misses imports made
lazily inside test function bodies, so real closures may be marginally wider.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

DECISIONS 2026-09-06 (user, answering the open questions in DESIGN):

1. ERROR POLICY: swallow-and-count. Edge recording catches, increments a counter
and keeps the first N exception reprs; both land in the profile so a degraded
graph is visible to so-jr5 rather than silently under-selecting. Costs one
documented noqa BLE001, matching the precedent in smoke_optimiser/plugin.py.

2. CODE LOCATION: a real typed module, smoke_optimiser/profiler/import_tracer.py,
imported normally. NOT the PYTEST_HOOK_CODE inline string. Decisive fact:
pyproject.toml already registers smoke_optimiser.plugin as a pytest11 entry
point, and the runner invokes sys.executable -m pytest, so smoke_optimiser is
ALREADY imported into every profiled run -- the dependency-free-subprocess
argument for the inline string is void. The win is unit-testability of the
edge-resolution arithmetic (level>1 relative imports becomes a 3-line test
rather than a nested fixture project run end to end), which matters because the
bug class here is a MISSING edge: it raises nothing and is invisible to an e2e
test.

3. MECHANISMS: implement BOTH the builtins.__import__ wrapper and the
sys.meta_path finder for importlib.import_module first-loads, in this issue.

4. XDIST: fix so-u3i FIRST, then implement edge capture consistently with the
write/merge path it establishes. so-u3i is now decided: support xdist, per-worker
files merged by the runner, runtime detection (not arg sniffing), worker count
recorded in the profile, and the TIME-based optimiser errors on a parallel
profile while map-only consumers stay silent.

IMPLEMENTATION DECISIONS 2026-09-06 (user), on top of the four already recorded:

5. THREE MECHANISMS, not two:
   - builtins.__import__ wrapper: every execution of an import statement, importer
     from globals["__name__"]. Primary.
   - importlib.import_module wrapper: import_module bypasses builtins.__import__
     entirely. Importer comes from the CALLER FRAME (sys._getframe), which is
     unambiguous at the call site, and it fires on every call rather than only on
     first load. Chosen over stack-walking inside find_spec, which would have to
     skip a variable number of importlib bootstrap frames and misattributes when
     the import happens inside a helper in another module.
   - sys.meta_path finder: the wider net for first loads through entry points
     neither wrapper sees (importlib.util, pkgutil, C-level __import__).

6. THE FINDER RECORDS LOADS, NOT EDGES. find_spec receives no globals, so it
   cannot know the importer, and NO frame heuristic is used to guess one. It
   records the module name only. At snapshot time any PROJECT module that was
   loaded but has zero importer edges is reported as unattributed_modules.
   so-jr5 must treat a change to one of those files as "cannot answer" -> run the
   full suite, NOT as "nothing imports it" -> select nothing. A wrong edge
   over-selects quietly; a missing edge under-selects silently, which is the exact
   failure this issue exists to prevent, so the blind spot is made loud instead of
   guessed at.

7. INSTALLED FROM THE PROFILING HOOK (_smoke_hook, passed with -p by the runner),
   not from the shipped smoke_optimiser/plugin.py. plugin.py is loaded by the
   pytest11 entry point into EVERY pytest run of every project that installs
   smoke-optimiser, so installing there would need an env-var gate to stay inert;
   the profiling-only plugin needs no gate and keeps profiling concerns out of the
   --smoke filter. Both are loaded at pytest startup, so both are early enough to
   precede collection.

8. XDIST: follows the path so-u3i established -- one graph file per worker,
   suffixed by PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER, unioned by the runner. Edges are a set, so the
   merge is a plain union; error and load counts sum.
close_reason: Import graph captured into the profile. Three-part graph (edges, unattributed_modules, resolution_errors) built from wrapping builtins.__import__ and importlib.import_module. Verified serial and under 3 xdist workers: identical 91-edge graph, all acceptance criteria covered by tests.

title: Files with no branches never appear in the coverage map, so change-based selection cannot see them
description:
ProfilingOutcome.branches_covered holds branch ids only. so-jr5 plans to invert
that map to get file -> tests, but a source file containing NO BRANCHES produces
no branch ids at all, so it is absent from the map entirely.

Straight-line code is common and exactly the kind that has no branches:
constants modules, __init__.py re-export files, dataclass and Pydantic model
definitions, thin delegating wrappers, protocol/ABC declarations. In this
repository smoke_optimiser/profiler/models.py and optimiser/models.py are both
pure declaration files.

CONSEQUENCE FOR so-jr5. Its fallback rule is 'a file with no entry in the map
means new code, so run everything'. A branchless file hits that rule and
triggers a full-suite run despite being neither new nor untested. The result is
SAFE but WRONG in its reasoning, and it fires on ordinary edits to model files,
which undermines the value of change-based selection precisely where it should
be cheapest. Worse, the fallback message will tell the user the file is new when
it is not.

NOTE THE ASYMMETRY: total_branches is derived from coverage's per-file analysis,
so a branchless file contributes nothing to the denominator either. Nothing is
miscounted -- the file is simply invisible.

OPTIONS.
1. Record a separate per-test file set alongside branches_covered, populated
   from the arc table's file_id for every executed arc regardless of whether it
   is a branch. Cheap: the ingest already streams every arc row, and the profile
   grows by roughly one path per test-file pair.
2. Distinguish 'file has no branches' from 'file not in the map' so so-jr5 can
   answer for branchless files without the full-suite fallback.

Option 1 also removes so-jr5's dependence on branch data for its file mapping,
which is a better fit for a feature whose granularity is deliberately
file-level.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/profiler/coverage_db.py::read_coverage_db (the per-arc
loop already has file_id in hand); smoke_optimiser/profiler/models.py for the
profile format.

ACCEPTANCE: a test that imports and calls into a branchless module can be found
by asking the map which tests touched that module's file.
close_reason: Added per-test files_covered and top-level measured_files to the profile

title: Coverage recorded during fixture setup aborts the entire profiling run
description:
REGRESSION introduced by so-mr0. A single test whose fixture executes measured source and then errors kills the whole profiling run.

REPRODUCED 2026-09-06 on a 2-test throwaway project:

  @pytest.fixture
  def broken():
      classify(-1)                 # exercises measured source during setup
      raise RuntimeError('boom')

  def test_setup_error(broken): ...

  $ smoke-optimiser --src app
  1 passed, 1 error in 0.02s
  ❌ Error: 1 coverage context matches no test that pytest collected in this run:
    test_edge.py::test_setup_error

WHY. coverage records a context per test PHASE, so the fixture's coverage lands
under 'test_edge.py::test_setup_error|setup'. But PYTEST_HOOK_CODE in
runner.py only records a report when report.when == 'call':

    if report.when == 'call':
        item.config._smoke_outcomes[item.nodeid] = {...}

A test that errors during setup never reaches its call phase, so it is absent
from test_durations. coverage_db._verify_contexts then finds a context matching
no collected test and raises, by design -- that fail-loudly check is correct and
should stay. The bug is that the test IS real and WAS collected; the hook simply
did not record it.

TWO THINGS ARE WRONG.
1. One errored fixture takes down a whole profiling run of any size.
2. The error message misdiagnoses it, telling the user the coverage database is
   stale and to 'remove it and profile again', which will fail identically.

NOT A PROBLEM: skipped tests, and setup errors in fixtures that touch no
measured source, both produce no context row at all (verified), so they do not
trigger this.

LIKELY FIX. Record setup/teardown phase reports in the hook so such tests appear
with passed=False. Failing tests are already hard-excluded by the optimiser
(PRD 5.5), so an errored test would be excluded by the existing path rather than
being a fatal ingest error. Needs a decision on duration (setup time only? zero?)
and on whether a teardown failure after a passing call should flip passed.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py PYTEST_HOOK_CODE; the check is
smoke_optimiser/profiler/coverage_db.py::_verify_contexts.

ACCEPTANCE: a suite containing a fixture that errors after touching measured
source profiles successfully, and tests/test_e2e.py covers it -- the current e2e
project has only cleanly-passing tests and would not catch this.
close_reason: Fixed by recording failed setup/teardown-phase reports in the pytest hook, so setup-erroring tests get an outcome entry instead of leaving an orphaned coverage context. Added regression coverage in tests/test_e2e.py.

title: Select tests from the map: turn a git diff and a profile into a test set
description:
smoke-optimiser's existing smoke mode selects a STATIC subset -- highest coverage
per second, the same tests whatever you changed. That is a coverage bet: it cannot
promise the coverage it skips, so it cannot gate a commit.

This is the second, honest selection mode. Given the files changed in the working
tree, run every test the profile says could be affected, and run the full suite
wherever the map cannot answer. The promise is categorical and literally statable,
which is the whole point: every test that has ever executed a line you touched,
plus every test that transitively imports a file you touched.

WHY IT IS POSSIBLE. The profiling data already IS a test-impact map.
ProfilingOutcome.files_covered gives file -> tests directly, and ImportGraph.edges
gives the dependency relation that answers for a file which only ever runs at
import time -- a constants module, a Pydantic model, a package re-export -- which
coverage records under no test context at all.

MEASURED on enphase_curtailer: 2600 tests, 190 files in the map, MEDIAN 37 TESTS
PER FILE. Touch one source file and you run ~37 of 2600. The full suite is 55s
warm on a 10-core Mac and 7m32s on GitHub CI's 4 cores.

GRANULARITY: FILE-LEVEL. Deliberately not line-level. Line numbers shift the moment
you insert a line above, so a line-level map silently mismatches after almost any
edit. File-level is immune to line shifts, reformatting and refactors within a
file. so-aif is the deferred line-level follow-up.

THE MAP MUST NEVER GUESS. Every input is either answered from recorded fact or
declared unanswerable, and unanswerable means the full suite with a stated reason.
There is no best-effort middle: the moment it selects a subset it cannot justify it
is test-fast again and cannot gate a commit.

SELF-HEALING. A full-suite fallback runs under profiling instrumentation and
rewrites the profile, so the run that pays for the fallback is also the run that
repairs the map. Instrumentation costs +11% (measured on enphase: 61s -> 68s), and
it means staleness costs one full run rather than accumulating until someone
remembers to regenerate by hand. Nothing regenerates in the background, and no
regeneration the developer did not ask for ever blocks a commit.

DOES NOT COVER, and must not pretend to: npm/vitest suites, tsc typechecks, codegen
drift checks, Rust. In casey_ai the heavy precommit item is a Docker integration
suite; only the Python half is in scope here.

This issue is the shared spec. Its children carry the work.
design:
THE INPUT is the union of staged, unstaged and untracked changes, because pytest
reads the worktree rather than the index: selecting on the index alone would test
something other than what is about to run. Renames are detected (-M) and resolved
to the OLD path, the only path the profile knows. A deleted file is looked up in
the map exactly like any other change -- the tests that executed it are the ones
most likely to break -- so nothing may gate on whether a path still exists on disk.

PATHS ARE REPO-RELATIVE throughout, from `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`, so the
profile and git agree by construction rather than by coincidence of the directory
smoke-optimiser was invoked from.

SELECTION for a changed file is the union of:
  - tests whose files_covered contains it (it executed under that test), and
  - tests whose module transitively imports it, via the inverted ImportGraph.

UNANSWERABLE -- run the full suite, and say which input caused it:
  - a changed path with no entry in the map (new code, which is exactly when tests
    matter most);
  - a changed path that is not Python at all (YAML, templates, assets, lockfiles,
    workflows). The map is a Python-execution map, so absence carries no
    information about a data file: it means "we never looked", not "nothing reads
    this". so-n6b.4 makes these answerable for real;
  - a changed file listed in ImportGraph.unattributed_modules, which means the
    graph is blind to who depends on it;
  - a profile whose map has never seen a file that exists now (see EXPIRY);
  - an import graph carrying failures we could not localise (see TRUST).

A CHANGED conftest.py selects every test at or below its directory, mirroring
pytest's own scoping rule, so a root conftest.py selects the whole suite and a
leaf one does not. A changed test file selects the tests in that file; a test file
that other tests import from is covered by the import graph like any other module.

EXPIRY is divergence, not age. A profile is expired once a file exists that its map
has never seen, because from that moment the map can answer confidently and wrongly:
the tests added since capture are absent from every answer it gives. Divergence is
a cliff rather than a slope, and the self-healing fallback is what makes the cliff
affordable -- hitting it costs one instrumented full run, not a full run on every
commit until someone regenerates by hand.

TRUST. The import tracer swallows and counts edge-resolution failures, because
raising inside __import__ would kill the suite being profiled. Every such failure
is our defect, not the project's -- it is our name arithmetic failing on legal
Python -- so the user must not be made to pay a full suite for it. The failure loses
the IMPORTED name while the IMPORTER is still in hand, so the doubt localises to
the importer: selection always additionally runs every test whose closure reaches a
module with a failed edge. Failures where even the importer could not be recovered
are counted separately and do force the full suite, since there is nothing to
localise them to.

OUTPUT is its own file with its own schema and its own pytest flag. The categorical
promise has no time cap, no coverage target and no efficiency ranking, so it shares
nothing with SmokeSuiteFile but the list of node ids.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, and rejected -- do not re-propose without new evidence:

  - Staged-only input (--cached). Rejected: pytest runs against the worktree, so an
    unstaged edit changes what the selected tests execute.
  - Treating a rename's new path as unknown, or forgoing -M so it appears as an
    add plus a delete. Both make every pure move cost a full suite.
  - A user-configurable ignore list for non-Python paths, so a README edit does not
    cost a full run. Rejected: "this path is irrelevant" is a claim that should be
    MEASURED, not asserted -- an asserted list is silent under-selection the moment
    it is wrong. so-n6b.3 measures it instead.
  - Wall-clock expiry with a configured threshold. Rejected: it is a heuristic that
    reads a day of heavy refactoring as fresh and an untouched fortnight as stale,
    while divergence measures the thing that actually breaks the map.
  - Refusing any profile with non-zero resolution_errors. Rejected: it punishes the
    user durably for our bug, since the failures are deterministic and persist
    until we fix the tracer.
  - Trusting a degraded graph with only a warning. Rejected: that is the silent
    under-selection this whole line of work exists to prevent.
  - Printing node ids for the caller to pass to pytest, with no file. Rejected: it
    puts a full suite's worth of argv on the command line at 2600 tests, and the
    fallback must run through our entry point for the self-healing rewrite to
    happen at all.
  - Regenerating the profile in a detached background process. Rejected: a full
    suite firing at an unpredictable moment is worse than the instrumented
    fallback, which pays the cost exactly when the developer was already paying it.
acceptance_criteria: Changing a source file runs exactly the tests that executed it plus the tests whose modules transitively import it, and no others. Changing a file absent from the map, a non-Python file, an unattributed module, or a file in a repository whose map has never seen some existing file, runs the full suite and names the input that caused it. Changing tests/sub/conftest.py runs every test under tests/sub/ and nothing outside it. A deleted file still selects the tests that executed it. A full-suite fallback rewrites the profile, so an immediately repeated run selects a subset instead of falling back again.
notes:
WHAT THE PROFILE PROVIDES, and what each part is for:

  - ProfilingOutcome.files_covered: every measured file a test executed, branchless
    files included, so a straight-line constants module is visible where
    branches_covered cannot see it.
  - ProfilingData.measured_files: everything coverage measured, executed or not, so
    "coverage never saw this file" is distinguishable from "no test ran it".
  - ImportGraph.edges: (importer, imported) as project-relative paths. Invert and
    take the transitive closure for every test module depending on a changed file.
  - ImportGraph.unattributed_modules: project files loaded that nothing was seen to
    import -- test modules, conftest.py, and any pytest11 plugin belonging to the
    project, since pytest loads entry-point plugins before any hook can watch. A
    change to one means the graph CANNOT ANSWER.
  - ImportGraph.resolution_errors / error_samples / failed_importers: edge recording
    that failed and was swallowed, because raising inside __import__ would kill the
    run being profiled.

Measured on smoke-optimiser itself: 91 edges, 17 unattributed of ~35 project files.

WHAT AN IMPORT CLOSURE SELECTS, as a percentage of the suite, per source file, from
a --collect-only prototype (2026-09-06):

  repo                tests  files   p25    median   p75    max     mean
  smoke-optimiser        81     19  18.5%   27.2%   48.1%  87.7%   33.3%
  casey_ai/api         1389    143  20.5%   47.7%   52.1%  96.5%   39.4%
  enphase_curtailer    2600    271   7.3%   12.8%   21.9%  93.2%   17.5%

The decisive case is casey_ai: db/models/common.py reaches 96.5% of the suite
(genuinely global -- running everything IS right), while db/models/interval.py and
db/models/task.py reach 3 tests each. Same directory, same kind of declaration file.
The graph tells them apart; a file-glob heuristic cannot.

CAVEAT: measured with --collect-only, so it misses imports made lazily inside test
bodies. Real closures may be marginally wider.
MVP, labelled touched-files-mvp: so-jr5.1, so-jr5.2, so-7hr, so-uom, so-jr5.4,
so-n6b.1, plus so-2os and so-qex. That is the whole path from a git diff to a pytest
run, with expiry included so the answer is trustworthy rather than merely fast.

It ships with three conservative stand-ins, each of which over-selects or errors
rather than under-selecting, and each of which is replaced by a named issue:

  - any changed conftest.py is unanswerable      -> so-017
  - any non-zero resolution_errors distrusts the graph -> so-n6b.2
  - the fallback runs plain pytest, regenerate by hand -> so-jr5.3
  - the command refuses to run outside the repository root -> so-746

Sequenced this way so the feature exists end to end early and gets exercised against
real edits, rather than being assembled correct-on-paper and met all at once.
close_reason: Superseded by so-n6b, which now carries this spec verbatim as its description, design and notes. Its children moved up to so-n6b: grouping by hierarchy was not carrying information, and the axis that matters is the touched-files-mvp label.

title: Replace the 1.2 GB JSON coverage ingest with a direct read of coverage.py's SQLite database
description:
smoke-optimiser cannot profile a medium suite today. Measured against
enphase_curtailer (2600 tests, 230 files) on 2026-09-06:

  coverage json --show-contexts    1.2 GB
  the same data as .coverage       29 MB      (40x smaller)
  the same report WITHOUT contexts 1.9 MB in 1.3s

parser.py:193 does a single json.load() of that 1.2 GB file, which needs many
GB of resident Python objects. The contexts are 99.8% of the file.

WHAT TO BUILD. Read coverage.py's SQLite database directly instead. One query
joining arc -> context -> file extracted the full test->arc map in 0.43s and
yielded exactly 2600 tests, matching the collected count:

  select context.context, file.path, arc.fromno, arc.tono
    from arc join context on arc.context_id = context.id
             join file    on arc.file_id    = file.id
   where context.context != ''

The public CoverageData API is NOT viable: set_query_contexts()/arcs() over 40
contexts took 6.51s, extrapolating to 13.4 minutes for this suite. Raw SQL is
~1900x faster. That is why this reads an internal schema.

TWO CORRECTNESS BUGS THIS FIXES.

1. parser.py:139 infers branch coverage: a test covers u->v if it executed line
   u and line v. That over-attributes -- both endpoints can execute without that
   arc ever being taken. The arc table holds real arcs, so the inference and its
   docstring caveat both go away.
2. TestResolver (parser.py:37-77) matches coverage contexts to node ids by
   endswith/startswith and by bare function name. Contexts are already exact node
   ids with a phase suffix ('tests/test_x.py::test_y|run'), so rsplit('|', 1)[0]
   is exact. The fuzzy matcher can mis-attribute coverage between same-named
   tests in different files; delete it.

SCHEMA COUPLING. The DB format is not a public API. Read the coverage_schema
table (version 7 as of coverage 7.13) and compare against a verified set. On a
mismatch, FAIL LOUDLY -- silently mis-reading would silently under-select tests,
which is the worst failure this tool can have. The error must name the schema
version found, the versions supported, the installed coverage.py version, and
say plainly that smoke-optimiser itself needs updating to support the new schema,
with the file to edit. Do not degrade quietly.

THE DENOMINATOR. The arc table records only arcs that were EXECUTED, so a
never-taken branch has no row. enphase has 3198 branches, 406 uncovered; counting
from SQLite alone reports 100% instead of 88%. --target-cov needs the true total,
so keep a SECOND context-free `coverage json` purely for totals -- 1.9 MB and 1.3s,
because the blow-up was entirely contexts. total_branches keeps its current
meaning (executed + missing).

Everything moves to the SQLite ingest, not just the new selection feature, so the
tool has one ingest path rather than two. Retire parse_coverage_json, TestResolver,
the CoverageReport/CoverageFile models, the [json] show_contexts rcfile setting,
and the contexts export step in runner.py:159-176.

Also handle a suite profiled WITHOUT branch mode: that data lands in line_bits
(a bitmap blob), not arc. Either support it or refuse with a clear message.
notes:
IMPLEMENTED with two departures from the original description, both agreed with the user.

1. NO SECOND coverage json. The description called for a context-free 'coverage json'
purely for the denominator. Not needed: the denominator is computed in-process from
coverage's own per-file analysis (FileReporter.arcs() filtered to branch lines), in the
same pass that builds the arc translation map. Measured 0.03s on this repo. Verified
byte-identical to 'coverage json' on both sets (denominator 234/234, executed 153/153),
and the 222-branch total matches pytest-cov's own report exactly. One ingest, no
subprocess, no JSON, no absolute-vs-relative path reconciliation between two sources.

2. RAW ARCS NEED TRANSLATING -- not mentioned in the original description, and the
landmine in it. The arc table records the interpreter's actual jump targets; coverage
reports branches in an AST-derived vocabulary. A jump into the middle of a multi-line
statement is reported against the statement's first line, so raw 3->6 is reported as
3->5. Intersecting raw arcs against reported branches without translation silently
dropped ~4% of this repo's executed branches -- exactly the silent under-selection the
issue exists to prevent. Fixed by running each file's distinct raw arcs through
FileReporter.translate_arcs ONCE, building a raw->branch lookup, then a dict hit per
arc. This is what sidesteps the 13.4-minute per-context path.

3. UNATTRIBUTABLE BRANCHES. Module-level code runs at import under the empty context,
so no test can ever claim it (4 branches on this repo). The old inference-based parser
falsely attributed these to whichever test touched the lines. They are now kept in
total_branches (so it keeps agreeing with 'coverage report') and surfaced as a new
ProfilingData.unattributable_branches field, with the summary reporting the attainable
ceiling: 'Ceiling: 98.2% max attainable'.

FAIL-LOUDLY paths, all tested: unsupported coverage_schema version (names version found,
supported set, installed coverage.py, and the file to edit), line-only data (has_arcs=0),
a context matching no collected test, a source file no longer readable, a corrupt or
non-coverage database, an empty coverage_schema table.

FOR so-jr5: branch ids are relative to project_root (POSIX), so they match git diff paths
directly. Note the file->test map only covers files that contain branches.
close_reason: Implemented: SQLite ingest with arc translation, in-process denominator, fail-loudly schema and context checks. Verified byte-identical to coverage json; 76 tests pass; ruff/ty clean.

title: (BUG) The unbounded-test-scope warning goes quiet for a project in a subdirectory
description:
`ProfileScope.collects_from_whole_repository` asks `WHOLE_REPOSITORY in
test_roots`, and `_warn_about_an_unbounded_test_scope` fires off it. That was
exact while the invocation directory was always the repository root: a project
configuring no `testpaths` left pytest pointed at the root, so the resolved test
root really was `.`.

It no longer is. pytest with no `testpaths` sets `config.args` to the invocation
directory, which now relativises to the project's offset -- `api`, not `.`. So a
subdirectory project that configures nothing gets `test_roots = {"api"}`, the
property answers False, and the warning never fires.

The project is in exactly the state the warning exists to describe: every `.py`
file beneath it is in scope, only files matching the test-file patterns can be
tracked, a new fixture or factory module goes unnoticed when the profile goes
stale, and any test-named file anywhere beneath it forces the full suite. None
of that is said.

The question the property is really asking is "was pytest pointed at a test
directory, or at the whole project?", and the answer is now "the test root
equals the project offset", of which `. == .` is the flat-layout case. The
profile records that offset as of so-746, so both halves are already in hand.

Verified by running pytest with no testpaths from a subdirectory: `ARGS:
['/private/tmp/scopechk/api'] ROOTDIR: /private/tmp/scopechk/api`.
acceptance_criteria: A project in a subdirectory of its repository that configures no testpaths gets the same unbounded-scope warning a project at the root does, and a project that configures testpaths still gets none.

title: Say so when a profile's coverage roots contain no Python at all
description:
A project whose resolved coverage roots contain no .py files at all profiles successfully and produces a profile that knows nothing. Every subsequent change then refuses to the full suite, forever, with no signal that adopting downwind was pointless for this repo.

A real example: vaultscribe is a Rust project with a Python test harness. Its src/ directory ships compiled binaries, not Python, so _discover_cov_target answers with src/ -- step 2 of the discovery order, a perfectly reasonable guess -- and instruments a directory containing nothing coverage can measure. Everything downstream behaves correctly. The profile is simply empty of anything useful, and the tool says so nowhere.

Refusal is the safe direction, so this is not a correctness bug. It is the difference between an adopter learning "downwind is not for this repo" in one run and concluding "downwind is mysteriously never selecting" over several weeks.

At the end of a profiling run, if the coverage roots walked to zero .py files, say so and name the roots. Sits naturally beside the existing refusal for a profile recording no scope roots at all -- same class of finding, same place, and that one already proves the shape of the message.
acceptance_criteria: Profiling a project whose coverage roots hold no .py files reports that, naming the roots, instead of writing a profile that silently knows nothing. A project with Python under its roots is unaffected.

title: Warn when the project's addopts carry --cov, so selective runs are not silently instrumented
description:
A project whose pytest addopts carry --cov instruments EVERY pytest run, including the selective one downwind fires on each commit. That is most of the saving gone, and it presents as "downwind isn't much faster than the full suite" rather than as anything diagnosable. A fallback is worse still: a second coverage session layers under the profiler's own.

This is a trap only the tool can see. pytest applies addopts inside the child process, so it is invisible from the command line an adopter reads. pytest_unconfigure already reaches the cov plugin's config to resolve scope, so the fact is in hand at exactly the moment a profiling run could report it.

Warn at profile time, naming the flags and saying where they belong: on the project's own full-suite test command, not in addopts, because addopts applies to runs that deliberately are not measuring coverage.

A real project hit this: casey_ai carries addopts = "--cov=. --cov-report=term-missing --cov-branch".

Distinct from so-n6b.26, which is about the PROFILING run receiving two --cov targets and measuring their union. This one is about every non-profiling run being instrumented at all. Same root cause, opposite end of the pipeline; the fix for either does not give the other.
acceptance_criteria: A profiling run whose child resolved a --cov it did not pass warns, names the flags, and says to move them to the full-suite test command. A project with no --cov in addopts is unaffected.

title: Document the CI-as-backstop pattern, and that the gitignored profile is load-bearing
description:
The README explains downwind as a precommit gate and explains the fallback, but never explains how the two combine into a working CI story -- and the combination is not obvious, because it is emergent rather than configured.

How it actually works, in the one project running it in anger: the profile is gitignored, so CI never has one. run_downwind loads the profile BEFORE it looks at the diff, so a missing profile short-circuits straight to _run_full_suite and a clean CI working tree never reaches the "clean tree, exit 0" branch. --no-regenerate-on-fallback then stops CI paying for instrumentation whose profile dies with the runner. One recipe, one env check, and CI is a genuine full-suite backstop with no second test step.

Two ways an adopter loses this without being told. They never derive it, and ship a CI that runs downwind against a tree with no diff -- which exits 0 having tested nothing. Or someone "helpfully" commits the profile, which silently converts CI's full suite into a selective run against a map that ages from that day on.

A README section -- "Using downwind as a precommit gate with CI as the backstop" -- giving the recipe and naming the gitignore entry as load-bearing rather than incidental. The ordering inside run_downwind is what makes it safe, so say so; it currently reads as an implementation detail and is in fact the guarantee.

Highest-value item in this epic: it is documentation of a design that already works, not new behaviour.
acceptance_criteria: The README shows the precommit-plus-CI recipe end to end, states why a missing profile runs the full suite before the diff is consulted, and warns that committing the profile silently downgrades CI to a selective run.

title: Close the adoption gaps downwind's second and third projects exposed
description:
Adopting downwind across a second and third project surfaced a cluster of gaps that are not bugs in selection -- the selection is right -- but in what the tool tells an adopter. Each one presents as "downwind is disappointing" rather than as an error, which is the worst shape a problem can take in a tool whose whole value proposition is a categorical guarantee.

The common thread: smoke-optimiser can see all of these and the adopter cannot. Coverage flags hidden in addopts, a coverage root containing no Python, a CI backstop that works only because of a gitignore entry nobody documented -- all of them are visible from inside the tool and invisible from outside it.

Sibling of so-746, which fixes the one true blocker adoption hit. This epic is everything else that exercise turned up.
acceptance_criteria: Each failure mode below either errors, warns, or is documented at the point an adopter would hit it; none of them present as 'downwind just isn't very good'.

title: A coverage root's package-walk exclusion narrows scope with no visible warning
description:
so-n6b.50 made _in_scope mirror coverage.py's package-walk rule: a subdirectory under a coverage root with no __init__.py (and include_namespace_packages not set) is excluded from scope, since coverage.py itself never measures it. This is correct, but it now silently narrows what a profile can ever know about -- a project with coverage_roots=["."] and a directory of plain scripts gets those files quietly excluded from scope, forever, with no indication to the user.

This project already treats this kind of silent narrowing as worth announcing: runner.py's HEURISTIC_COV_SOURCES/_announce_cov_source comment says "a run that quietly widened the coverage root from a package to the whole repository is how a profile acquires files coverage can never measure... with them an expiry no amount of regenerating clears", and _warn_about_an_unbounded_test_scope (runner.py) already warns when pytest's test root is the whole repository, for the parallel reason.

Files affected by the package-walk rule get no equivalent warning. A user who intended full coverage under "." would have no way to discover that a directory of scripts is invisible to their profile, or why a change there never gets a test selection.

Design questions this needs (hence model:opus, not a mechanical fix):
- Where to compute this: resolve_scope (smoke_optimiser/profiler/scope.py) is documented as pure and runs inside the profiled subprocess; producing a warning there would need to change that contract, or the check could be redone at the orchestration layer (runner.py) where _warn_about_an_unbounded_test_scope already lives.
- What to report: which directories were excluded, or just a count/one example, given a large monorepo could have many.
- Whether this should be a warning (like the existing test-scope one) or something recorded in the profile/downwind output so it surfaces at select time too, not just at profiling time.

title: The read map drops every .py read, so a test that opens a source file is attached to it by nothing
description:
`_record_read` in profiler/read_tracer.py drops every path ending `.py`, on the stated
grounds that coverage and the import graph already record Python. That holds for a module a
test IMPORTS. It does not hold for a source file a test OPENS as data -- an architecture rule
that parses the tree, a lint of the sources, a test asserting a file's contents -- where
coverage sees nothing, the import graph sees nothing, and the read map deliberately throws
the one observation that exists away.

Harmless while an unknown Python file forced the full suite. so-n6b.54 changed that: a
Python file present during the run and absent from every map now selects only the tests
that LISTED its directory. A test that globs before it opens is still attached, which is the
common shape and why the listers are unioned in there. A test that opens a hardcoded path --
`Path("src/registry.py").read_text()` -- lists nothing, so nothing connects it to the file
any more.

The fix is to stop filtering: record a `.py` read like any other, and let the read map's
file -> tests relation carry it. The rules need no change, because a Python path never
reaches `_read_answer` -- what changes is that `tests_reading(path)` has an answer for an
inert module, and the inert rule can union it in beside the listers.

The cost is volume, and it is why the filter is there. Every import opens a `.py`, so the
map grows by roughly one entry per module per test, and most of that is already said by
coverage. Worth measuring before choosing: filtering by whether the read happened during an
import (the tracer knows whether it is inside an import hook) would keep the signal and drop
the bulk.

title: The full-suite fallback promises to rebuild the map even for blind spots re-profiling can never clear
description:
The fallback prints "Running the full suite under instrumentation, so this run rebuilds the
map it fell back from" for every refusal, and for several blind spots that is false: the
next run reproduces exactly the same refusal, and the developer pays a full suite each time
with a message telling them it is being fixed.

so-n6b.54 was one instance -- a Python file no recorder can see -- and it was reported as
"no matter how many times I run and profile, it's still running the entire suite". The
message is why the loop was invisible: it names a repair that is not happening.

Which reasons re-profiling can clear is a property of the reason, and the vocabulary in
downwind/blind_spots.py is where it belongs, beside the reasons themselves. EXPIRED_PROFILE
and a genuinely new UNKNOWN_PATH clear on the next run and are what the fallback exists for.
UNATTRIBUTED_IMPORT and TERMINAL_DEAD_END do not: a plugin the tracer cannot attribute is
unattributable again tomorrow. RESOLUTION_ERRORS and READ_ERRORS depend on why the recorder
failed, which nothing currently records. CHANGED_CONFTEST and ENVIRONMENT_FILE are not map
faults at all -- they refuse on purpose, and instrumenting the suite for them buys nothing.

Two things follow. The message must be conditional on the refusal actually containing
something a rewrite can repair, and a refusal made only of reasons re-profiling cannot clear
should say what the developer would have to change instead -- which is the only action
available to them.

Whether such a run should still be instrumented is a separate question and probably yes: the
suite is running anyway and a fresh profile is worth having. What must stop is claiming the
rewrite addresses the reason it fell back for.

title: A subprocess-invoked script is invisible to every tracer, so the inertness rule under-selects for it
description:
A `.py` file a test runs through `subprocess` is opened by a child interpreter. Neither
the audit hook nor coverage is installed there, so the read map and the import graph are
both blind to it, and the parent process's only trace of it is the `subprocess.Popen`
audit event -- which the read tracer does not listen for.

This was tolerable while an unknown Python file forced the full suite. so-n6b.54 makes a
Python file that was present and appears in no map select only the tests that listed its
directory, so a subprocess-invoked script now goes from over-selecting to selecting
almost nothing. That is the one under-selection the inertness rule admits, and this is
what closes most of it.

`subprocess.Popen` carries the argv. Any element of it that resolves to a repository
path can be attributed to the active test exactly as a read is, which covers the common
shapes -- `[sys.executable, "scripts/x.py"]`, `["./scripts/x.py"]`, `[sys.executable,
"-m", "pkg.module"]` needing a module-to-file resolution of its own.

The `.py` filter in `_record_read` stays: this is a new relation, not a widening of the
read map, because what it records is "a test ran this file", not "a test read it".

title: cov_source carries one value where coverage takes many, and the note saying so is never shown
description:
ResolvedConfig.cov_source, ProfilingRunConfig.cov_source and FileConfig.cov_source are each a single str, and _build_pytest_command emits one --cov from it. coverage.py takes a list, and projects use it: [tool.coverage.run] source = ["app", "lib"] is ordinary.

Three consequences, in increasing order of how quietly they go wrong:

1. _cov_target_from_coverage_config takes declared[0] and builds a DiscoveredCovSource.note saying only the first of N entries is used. NOTHING EVER PRINTS THAT NOTE. ProfilingRunConfig carries value and origin but not the note, and _announce_cov_source only renders the origin. So the field is computed, tested, and dead -- and a project with two coverage sources is silently profiled against one of them, which is exactly the "silently narrower than you asked for" failure the announcement exists to prevent.

2. A profile recording several coverage_roots cannot be reproduced by a downwind fallback. _coverage_source in downwind/command.py reuses the replaced profile root only when there is exactly one, and otherwise falls through to a guess -- so the projects most likely to have a wide, deliberate scope are the ones whose fallback silently re-guesses it.

3. The scope a profile records is already a frozenset of roots, so the profile side of this is correct and only the config side is lossy. The two disagree about the shape of the same fact.

Fixing it means cov_source becoming a sequence through ResolvedConfig, ProfilingRunConfig and DownwindConfig, _build_pytest_command emitting one --cov per entry, and a decision about the CLI: --src is a single-valued option today, so either it becomes repeatable or the file config becomes the only way to name several. reports/repro.py emits --src and has a completeness test, so it moves too.

The dead note should be deleted or surfaced as part of this -- leaving it computed and unread is the worst of the three states.
acceptance_criteria: A project declaring several coverage sources is profiled against all of them, and a fallback reproduces all of them. No path silently reduces a multi-source configuration to its first entry; if any still must, it says so where the user can see it. DiscoveredCovSource carries no field that nothing renders.

title: Coverage configuration is only read from pyproject.toml, so a .coveragerc project is refused outright
description:
so-jr5.3 made _discover_cov_target read the project own coverage configuration ahead of every guess, and made a source nobody chose refuse to profile rather than default to the whole repository. Both are right, but discovery reads only [tool.coverage.run] in pyproject.toml (config.py, _cov_target_from_coverage_config).

coverage.py itself reads its configuration from several places: .coveragerc, setup.cfg and tox.ini (under [coverage:run]), and whatever --cov-config names. A project that configures source or source_pkgs in any of those looks, to us, exactly like a project that configured nothing.

The consequence is worse than it was before so-jr5.3. Such a project used to get a whole-repository profile and a warning; it now gets a hard refusal telling it to set cov_source -- a setting it has already set, somewhere we do not look. The error message names [tool.smoke_optimiser] and --src and never mentions the file the project actually used, so it reads as the tool failing to notice.

Where: smoke_optimiser/config.py, _read_pyproject and _cov_target_from_coverage_config. The precedence between several config files needs deciding rather than inheriting: coverage own order is --cov-config, then .coveragerc, then setup.cfg, then tox.ini, then pyproject.toml, and ours should not disagree with it.

Note this is discovery of WHAT TO MEASURE only. so-asl covers the separate problem that the generated rcfile replaces the project coverage configuration during the run.
acceptance_criteria: A project declaring its coverage source in .coveragerc, setup.cfg or tox.ini is discovered rather than refused, and the announcement names the file the value came from. The precedence between the files matches coverage.py own order. A project that genuinely configures nothing anywhere is still refused.

title: Top up a profile's iterations instead of re-running the whole suite from scratch
description:
A profile records how many complete passes its durations are the mean of (ProfilingMeta.iterations, added in so-jr5.3). When the optimiser is asked to rank a profile holding fewer samples than the project configured, it should run the SHORTFALL -- two more passes over a 1-iteration profile where iterations = 3 -- and merge them into what is already there, rather than discarding the existing samples and running all three again.

The case that makes this worth having: a downwind full-suite fallback profiles the suite once, whatever the project configured, because iterations exist to average durations and only the optimiser reads durations. The maps come out identical on every pass, so a second one would cost the developer another full suite for nothing they are waiting on. That leaves a correct profile that is thinner than the project asked for, and today the only way to thicken it is to re-run every pass.

WHAT MAKES IT MORE THAN AN ARITHMETIC CHANGE:

- Coverage accumulates into a database that currently lives in a TemporaryDirectory and is deleted with it (runner.run_profiling). Merging a later pass into an earlier one means that database, or an equivalent, has to outlive the run that made it -- which is new machinery, and a new artefact to decide the lifetime, location and staleness rules of.
- Averaging a top-up correctly needs the per-test sample COUNTS, not just the means: a test present in one pass and absent from another cannot be re-averaged from the mean alone. Either the profile records counts per test, or the top-up recomputes from retained per-pass durations.
- The tree may have changed between the original pass and the top-up. Durations merged across two different trees are a different fact from durations averaged across two passes over one tree, and ProfilingMeta.commit names only one of them. Related to the same question in so-n6b.17.

Until this exists, a profile recorded by a fallback simply ranks on one sample. That is a worse ranking, not a wrong map, and downwind selection is unaffected either way.
acceptance_criteria: Ranking a profile that holds fewer samples than configured runs only the shortfall and merges it, leaving meta.iterations at the configured number. A top-up over a tree that has changed since the original pass is either refused or recorded as such, rather than silently averaging durations from two different codebases.

title: A profile write killed part-way destroys the profile it was replacing
description:
save_profile (smoke_optimiser/profiler/persistence.py) destroys the old profile before it
has written the new one:

    profile_path.unlink(missing_ok=True)
    with profile_path.open("w") as f:
        json.dump(file_data.model_dump(mode="json"), f)

A process killed anywhere in that window leaves either no profile at all or a truncated
one. Both are worse than the profile that was there a moment earlier: downwind treats an
absent profile as "run the full suite" and a corrupt one as a hard error, and in neither
case can it get back the good profile it had.

The window is not narrow. model_dump walks every test's branch and file sets, and json.dump
streams the result, so a large suite's profile is a long write -- and the runs most likely
to be killed are exactly the long ones.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE NOW. Until so-n6b.25 only --profile-only wrote the file, so the
exposure was limited to a command the user ran deliberately and could simply run again.
Every smoke run now writes it, so an interrupted ordinary run can take the profile with it.

THE FIX. Write to a temporary file beside the target and os.replace it into position, which
is atomic on POSIX and on Windows. The unlink then goes away with it: replace overwrites,
and unlinking first is what opens the window in the first place.

so-jr5.3 requires that a fallback which did not produce complete data leaves the previous
profile in place. That is a condition on whether to write at all; this is the guarantee
that writing does not destroy the previous profile on its way. so-jr5.3 needs both.
acceptance_criteria: The profile is written to a temporary file and moved into place, so an interrupted write leaves the previous profile intact and readable. No window exists in which the target path is absent or partially written.
close_reason:
Fixed by staging the write to a sibling .tmp and os.replace-ing it into position, so the target path is never absent or half-written and a killed write leaves the previous profile intact and readable.

Regression test in tests/test_persistence.py (new module) simulates a failed write and asserts the previous profile survives it, both as bytes and through load_profile. Verified it fails against the previous code.

One consequence recorded on so-n6b.47: a hard kill now leaves a .smoke_profiling_data.json.tmp behind, since no cleanup can run. That is the right trade for not losing the profile, but it adds another untracked artefact to the set that issue is about.

title: A symlinked repository path makes the read tracer record nothing, silently
description:
ReadTracer resolves the project root once (read_tracer.py, __init__: Path(project_root).resolve()) and then rejects any absolute event path that does not start with it. That fast path is a plain string comparison, chosen deliberately so the hot path stays free of allocation -- the overwhelming majority of a suite's opens are absolute paths into site-packages.

The comparison is between a RESOLVED root and an UNRESOLVED event path, so the two disagree whenever the repository is reached through a symlink. On macOS this is not exotic: /tmp is a symlink to /private/tmp, and a checkout under a symlinked home or work directory behaves the same way. Root resolves to /private/tmp/repo while a test opening Path(__file__).parent / 'fixtures/a.yaml' can produce /tmp/repo/fixtures/a.yaml, which fails startswith and is dropped.

Relative paths are unaffected: Path.cwd() returns the physical path, so they resolve against the same root. It is absolute paths derived from pytest's rootdir or from __file__ that are at risk.

The failure is the worst class this tool has. Nothing errors, the profile simply records fewer reads than really happened, and downwind then answers 'measured as unread -> select nothing' for a fixture tests genuinely read. Under-selection with no symptom.

Fix needs care about cost: resolving every event path would put a symlink syscall inside every open of the profiled suite. Better candidates are comparing against BOTH the resolved and the unresolved root, or resolving the root the way the event paths are spelled. Whatever is chosen, it must not turn the fast path into a syscall.

title: Record non-Python file reads during profiling to narrow the non-Python blind spot
description:
Every changed file that is not .py is an unconditional NON_PYTHON_FILE blind spot (see _blind_spot_reason in downwind/rules.py), forcing the full suite regardless of whether any test could plausibly be affected -- a changed Justfile, README, or CI config triggers it exactly like a changed Jinja template would. Since profiling only instruments Python execution, there is currently no way to know whether a non-Python file was ever read by anything, so the rule has to assume the worst.

Fix: during profiling, register a sys.addaudithook on the 'open' event (covers open(), os.open, io.open) and record which paths get opened while each test's coverage context is active -- mirroring the per-test context switching coverage_db.py already reads for branches. Store the result as a new per-test files_read set in the profile, parallel to files_covered.

With that recorded, _blind_spot_reason can stop treating every non-Python file the same way: one nothing ever opened during profiling is provably irrelevant and should not be a blind spot at all; one some tests did open should map to just those tests instead of falling back to the whole suite.
design: Touches the profile schema (PROFILE_SCHEMA_VERSION bump, new field on ProfilingOutcome, migration/back-compat handling in persistence.py) and downwind's DownwindMaps/rules. Needs care around: audit hook overhead across a full suite run; noise from files opened outside any test context (module-level/session-scope reads, which should probably fall into the same unattributed/import-time bucket the Python side already has); and matching path normalisation against the existing project-relative scheme. This loosens the project's stated blind-spot invariant (every reason over-selects, never under-selects) for the specific case of a provably-unread file, which is worth flagging explicitly in review rather than treating as a silent side effect of the instrumentation change.

comments.author: lawther
comments.text: Superseded by so-n6b.3 (capture: the audit hook and the per-test read map) and so-n6b.4 (consume: replacing the NON_PYTHON_FILE rule). Both predate this card and carry the verified mechanism, the exclusion list, the xdist merge and the alternatives already ruled out. The two points unique to this card were folded in: the PROFILE_SCHEMA_VERSION bump and persistence handling into so-n6b.3, and the requirement to rewrite the blind_spots.py over-selection invariant explicitly into so-n6b.4. This card also omitted the fixed full-suite carve-out for environment-defining files (uv.lock, pyproject.toml, Dockerfiles), which so-n6b.4 keeps and lawther confirmed on 2026-09-08.

title: Suggest a single glob omit pattern for multiple unparseable measured files
description: When read_coverage_db finds several measured files that are not Python source (typically templates a templating engine compiled under their own filename), the warning from _warn_about_unparseable_files just lists every offending path. It should instead compute the smallest number of glob patterns (relative to the project root) that cover the whole list -- ideally one, e.g. a shared directory plus extension such as app/templates/**/*.html -- and print a ready-to-paste [tool.coverage.run] omit entry using those patterns, the same way the current single-file NotPython message already does for one file.
design: Group unparseable_files by directory and extension. A reasonable first pass: find the common parent directory of all the paths and suggest a single recursive glob for that directory plus the set of extensions seen (e.g. omit = ["app/templates/**/*.html"]); fall back to per-file entries only if the files don't share a sensible common root or extension. Needs care around glob syntax coverage.py actually accepts (fnmatch-style, ** for recursive) -- verify against coverage's own omit matching before committing to a pattern shape.

title: save_profile hand-maps every field, so a new one on ProfilingData is silently not persisted
description:
smoke_optimiser/profiler/persistence.py save_profile() converts ProfilingData into
ProfilingDataFile by naming all forty-odd fields one at a time -- MachineModel from
MachineEnvironment, ProfilingMetaModel from ProfilingMeta, ProfilingOutcomeModel per test,
ImportGraphModel from ImportGraph, then ProfilingDataFile itself. Add a field to any of those
dataclasses and this function keeps compiling, keeps passing, and quietly writes a profile
without it.

That failure is not hypothetical for this codebase: 'scope' was added to ProfilingData in
so-n6b.1 and had to be threaded through here by hand, and 'unattributable_branches' before it.
Each one was a place the author had to remember.

NOTHING WOULD CATCH IT. tests/test_profiler_models.py::test_profiling_data_roundtrip covers
only the READ direction -- a raw dict through ProfilingDataFile to ProfilingData. There is no
test that takes a fully-populated ProfilingData, writes it, reads it back and asserts the two
are equal, so the write direction is entirely unexercised as a mapping.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE NOW: the profile is no longer just a resume point for --optimise-init.
It is the artefact the downwind maps are built from, so a field dropped on write is a fact
the maps then answer without -- confidently and wrongly, which is the one failure mode the
downwind line of work exists to prevent.

TWO PARTS, and the first is worth doing even if the second is rejected:
1. A round-trip test over a ProfilingData with every field populated to a distinctive value:
   save it, load it, assert equality. That turns a silent omission into a failing test.
2. Consider whether the hand-mapping is needed at all. The models are structurally parallel to
   the dataclasses; whether that can be exploited (a shared construction, or generating the
   file models from the dataclasses) or whether the two shapes genuinely need to differ --
   frozenset versus list, for one -- is the design question here.

comments.text: Hit again on 2026-09-08 adding files_read/directories_listed/reads/present_files for so-n6b.3. title: CLI-supplied config values bypass every FileConfig validator
description:
FileConfig declares real constraints -- time_cap ge=0, target_cov ge=0 le=100, iterations ge=1 --
and they are enforced only for values that arrive from pyproject.toml. A value from the
command line is written over the model without ever being validated, so every one of those
constraints is silently optional depending on where the setting came from.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/config.py _apply_cli_overrides(). It builds the stated overrides and
applies them with base.model_copy(update=stated), and model_copy deliberately does not
re-validate. The same hole existed before that helper was extracted -- the old code assigned
straight into a model_dump() dict -- so this is long-standing rather than new, but it is now
in one place and fixable in one place.

CONCRETELY:

  smoke-optimiser smoke --iterations=0     # accepted; the profiling loop runs zero times
  smoke-optimiser smoke --target-cov=500   # accepted; a target no suite can reach
  smoke-optimiser smoke --time-cap=-5      # accepted

Typer converts the type but asserts nothing about the range, so nothing else catches these.
--iterations=0 is the nastiest: run_profiling's loop body never executes, so there are no
outcomes, no coverage database, and the failure surfaces much later as an ingest error about
a missing database rather than as 'zero is not a number of iterations'.

WHAT NEEDS DECIDING, which is why this is not a one-line change. Constructing
FileConfig(**(base.model_dump() | stated)) validates, but the ValidationError then reaches
cli.py's _report_invalid_configuration, whose message says 'Invalid configuration in
pyproject.toml' -- exactly wrong for a value the user typed. The fix needs to tell the two
sources apart and say which one it is unhappy about, ideally naming the flag rather than the
model field. Typer's own callback validation is the alternative, at the cost of restating each
constraint beside the flag, where it can drift from the model's.

title: Untracked __pycache__/*.pyc files force the full suite on any project that does not gitignore them
description:
changed_files runs 'git status --untracked-files=all', so every untracked file in the
tree is in the changed set. On a project that does not gitignore __pycache__, that
includes one .pyc per imported module -- each of which is a non-Python file, each of
which raises a NON_PYTHON_FILE blind spot, and so every downwind run refuses and runs
the full suite. The tool never selects anything, and the reason it gives is a wall of
.pyc paths rather than anything the developer recognises as their problem.

Found while building the so-jr5.4 fixture project, which had to add __pycache__/ to its
.gitignore before a selection was possible at all.

Most projects do gitignore __pycache__, which is why this is a sharp edge rather than a
blocker. But 'you must configure your .gitignore correctly or this tool silently never
works' is a bad failure mode for a precommit gate, and the symptom does not name its own
cause.

WHAT TO DECIDE. A .pyc is not a data file the project reads -- it is derived from a .py
the maps already know -- so it is arguably not the kind of file so-n6b.3's 'measure what
each test reads' rule is about, and a fixed rule excluding Python's own build artefacts
would not be the user-configurable ignore list the epic rejected. Alternatively the
refusal could simply say 'these look like build artefacts; gitignore them', which fixes
the diagnostic without adding a rule.

NOT the same as so-n6b.3, which makes a genuinely-read data file answerable. This is
about a file nothing reads and nothing should ever have been asked about.
close_reason:
Not a bug any more, and it was fixed by the read map rather than by anything aimed at it.

The body is written against NON_PYTHON_FILE, a reason that no longer exists. A .pyc now goes through _read_answer like any other non-Python path: nothing read it, nothing listed __pycache__, so it selects nothing instead of refusing. so-n6b.54's widening of the denominator reaches the same answer by the other branch when the .pyc predates the run.

Measured on a fixture repo with no .gitignore at all: an edit to src/app.py reported five changed files, four of them .pyc, and still selected '1 of 1 tests downwind' with no blind spot and no full suite. The failure this issue exists to describe cannot be reproduced.

Two adjacent things were noticed and deliberately not carried forward here, because neither is what this issue says: the changed-file list is mostly artefact noise a developer reads past, which so-n6b.47 now covers on its own terms, and read_tracer's EXCLUDED_PATH_PARTS is a second hand-rolled definition of 'not a project file' sitting beside git's, which is worth its own issue if it ever bites.

comments.text:
Measured today against a throwaway fixture repo with no .gitignore at all: an edit to src/app.py reported 5 changed files -- four of them .pyc under __pycache__ -- and still selected '1 of 1 tests downwind', with no blind spot and no full suite.

The symptom this issue describes cannot happen any more. Two things could still be judged worth doing, and neither is what the body says: the changed-file list is mostly artefact noise a developer has to read past, and read_tracer's EXCLUDED_PATH_PARTS is a second, hand-rolled definition of 'not a project file' sitting beside git's. If either is the live work, the body needs rewriting to say so; otherwise this is closable.

title: A conftest hook's reach is invisible to coverage, so a fixture-using conftest under-selects the tests it only hooks
description:
Pre-existing, and deliberately left in place by so-n6b.29's 'only when barren' trigger. Filed because it is a SILENT under-selection, the one failure the epic exists to prevent.

downwind/rules.py:_tests_downwind_of falls back to conftest directory scope only when a terminal conftest yields no tests by either relation. Under --cov=. it usually yields some, because fixture bodies run inside the using test's setup context and coverage records them there. The fallback then does not fire and coverage's answer is taken as complete.

It is not complete. A conftest's COLLECTION-time code -- pytest_collection_modifyitems, pytest_generate_tests, module-level constants, anything outside a fixture or hook wrapper -- runs under no test context at all, so it appears in the .coverage file table under the empty context and in no test's files_covered. Its reach is therefore invisible to tests_executing.

The shape that bites: tests/conftest.py imports src/settings.py and uses it BOTH in a fixture some tests request AND in pytest_collection_modifyitems that affects every test in the directory. Change src/settings.py, and the closure terminates at the conftest, which yields the fixture's users. Those are selected; every test affected only through the hook is silently dropped.

Only --cov=. projects are exposed. A --cov=pkg project never measures the conftest at all, so both relations answer empty, the fallback fires and directory scope covers the hook's reach by accident.
design:
The trigger is the decision to re-open, not the fallback itself: directory scope is already the right answer here, it simply does not fire.

Options:
* Fire directory scope whenever a terminal conftest DEFINES a collection-time hook, keeping the precise coverage answer for a conftest that is only fixtures. Needs the profiler to record which conftests declare hooks, since the rules are pure and cannot read the file.
* Fire directory scope for every terminal conftest, dropping the 'only when barren' condition. Trivially correct and loses the precision so-n6b.29 chose to keep -- measure how much precision that actually is on a --cov=. project before assuming it matters.
* Have the profiler attribute the empty coverage context of a conftest to the tests collected under it, which is directory scope computed a layer earlier.

Whichever wins, so-n6b.29's rationale in the rules.py module docstring and so-017's design note contrasting the two triggers both need rewriting to match.
acceptance_criteria: A hand-built profile where a conftest is measured, yields tests via coverage for a fixture, and imports a module its collection-time code also uses, does not return a selection omitting the tests the conftest only hooks. Both the fixture-only conftest case and the hook case get their own unit test, so whichever precision is kept is pinned rather than incidental.

title: A test skipped while profiling is absent from the profile, so downwind can never select it
description:
