The profiling hook records a test only from its 'call' phase, plus setup/teardown FAILURES (smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py, pytest_runtest_makereport in PYTEST_HOOK_CODE). A skipped test never reaches 'call' and its setup did not fail, so it lands in no outcomes file and is absent from ProfilingData.tests entirely.

Downwind selection reads that dict for both of its relations, so a test skipped at capture time can never appear in any answer. It is not merely unranked -- it does not exist to the maps.

WHY IT MATTERS: skips are conditional, and the condition at profile time need not hold at run time. casey_ai/api marks its integration tests 'auto-skipped when no Docker daemon is available'. Profile on a laptop with Docker down, then run pytest --downwind on CI where Docker is up: the integration tests are silently absent from the selection, while the full suite would have run them. The promise the epic makes -- every test that has ever executed a line you touched, plus every test whose module transitively imports it -- quietly excludes them, and nothing in the output says so. Same class as so-n6b.24, arriving through a different door: there the run was truncated, here it completed and simply did not record part of itself.

A SECOND EFFECT, in so-jr5.2's rules: the unattributed exemption in smoke_optimiser/downwind/rules.py fires only when tests_in_module(path) is non-empty. A test module whose tests were ALL skipped has no node ids recorded, so it reads as an unattributed module with no tests and refuses with UNATTRIBUTED_IMPORT. That direction is safe -- a full suite, not a silent omission -- but it is the wrong reason, and a developer editing that file is told the import graph is blind when the real problem is that the profile never saw the tests.

Skipped tests also inflate nothing in smoke mode, since the optimiser cannot select what is not there, but the same absence means a suite whose skips vary by environment profiles differently on every machine.
design:
The open question is what a skipped test's record should contain, and it needs deciding before implementation. It has no duration worth trusting and no coverage at all, so it cannot be a ProfilingOutcome like any other -- giving it duration 0.0 and an empty files_covered would make it a free, useless test to the smoke optimiser's efficiency ranking. Downwind needs only its node id and the file it is defined in, which is strictly less than an outcome carries.

Options: a separate 'skipped' collection on ProfilingData that only the downwind maps read; an outcome with an explicit skipped flag that the optimiser filters out; or recording it in the maps' tests_in_module relation alone, which is where downwind reads it from anyway. All three touch the profile schema, so so-n6b.16's version bump applies.
acceptance_criteria: A test skipped during the profiling run is present in the profile, distinguishable from one that ran, and reachable by downwind selection when its module is downwind of a change. A test module whose tests were all skipped is not reported as an unattributed import. The smoke optimiser does not treat a skipped test as a candidate with a real duration.

title: A corrupt or unreadable pyproject.toml is silently treated as no configuration at all
description:
load_file_config (smoke_optimiser/config.py) catches OSError and tomllib.TOMLDecodeError and returns None. None means 'this project has no [tool.smoke_optimiser] section', so the run proceeds on defaults as though the user had configured nothing.

A stray quote or an unclosed bracket anywhere in pyproject.toml therefore discards every setting the project has -- time_cap, target_cov, include_mandatory, the lot -- without a word. The user gets a plausible-looking run built from defaults they never chose.

The file is inconsistent with itself on this point, which is the clearest argument that it is wrong:
  - load_file_config: unparseable file -> silent None, defaults used.
  - _discover_cov_target: hits the SAME two exception types on the SAME file and emits a yellow warning to stderr before falling back.
  - Invalid VALUES (e.g. target_cov = 101) raise ValidationError, which cli.py catches and reports as a red error listing each bad field, exiting 1.

So an out-of-range number is a loud fatal error, while a malformed file that hides that same number is silent. The strictest treatment is reserved for the case the user can most easily see.

WHY THIS GATES THE DOWNWIND EPIC. so-jr5.4 states that 'a configuration surface that silently ignores pyproject.toml would make the rules behave differently from how the project asked', and it is the command a precommit hook calls. The epic's governing rule is that the maps never guess -- every input is answered from recorded fact or declared a blind spot. Silently substituting default configuration for the project's own is precisely the guess that rule forbids, and it happens before the maps are ever consulted, so no blind-spot machinery can catch it. A commit gate that reads a corrupt config and proceeds on defaults is a gate nobody can trust.

FIX: a pyproject.toml that exists but cannot be parsed should be a hard error -- red message naming the file and the parse failure, exit 1 -- matching how invalid values are already handled in cli.py. A file that does not exist stays None; that genuinely means 'no configuration'. Distinguish the two rather than collapsing them.

Keep OSError separate in the message from TOMLDecodeError: unreadable and unparseable are different problems for the user to act on.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/config.py, load_file_config's try/except; the caller is cli.py in main, already inside a try that reports configuration errors.

title: FileConfig.smoke_file_path is inert: a documented pyproject key that nothing ever reads
description:
smoke_file_path is declared in FileConfig (smoke_optimiser/config.py:29) and read nowhere. Nothing else in the codebase mentions it.

The pytest plugin gets its path from its OWN option parser instead: plugin.py:35 registers --smoke-file-path via pytest_addoption, and plugin.py:61 and plugin.py:208 read it back with config.getoption. It never loads FileConfig at all.

So a project that sets

  [tool.smoke_optimiser]
  smoke_file_path = "build/smoke.json"

is validated, parsed, dropped, and ignored. pytest --smoke goes on reading ./.smoke_suite.json. The setting looks supported and does nothing.

This is documented as supported in two places, which is what makes it a bug rather than dead code: PRD-smoke-optimiser.md:129 lists it in the configuration table with a CLI flag and a default, and README.md documents --smoke-file-path in the plugin arguments table.

Note this is the SAME failure class as so-qex -- a configuration surface that accepts a setting and silently declines to honour it -- but a distinct mechanism. so-qex was a precedence bug in resolve_config; this key never reaches resolve_config at all (ResolvedConfig has no such field).

DECIDE WHICH WAY TO FIX, they are not equivalent:
  (a) Make the plugin honour pyproject.toml -- load FileConfig in pytest_configure and use smoke_file_path as the default for --smoke-file-path, so the flag still wins. This is what the docs currently promise. Note the plugin runs inside the user's pytest process, so it must not be expensive or throw on a malformed file.
  (b) Delete the field and correct both documents, if per-project configuration of this path is not actually wanted.

Whichever is chosen, --downwind-file-path (plugin.py:98, plugin.py:221) has the same shape and should be settled at the same time rather than left to diverge.

VERIFIED, not theorised: grep for smoke_file_path across the tree returns exactly the one declaration and no readers.

title: A truncated run (-x, --maxfail) exits 1, so the suite is profiled as though it finished
description:
so-2os made the runner reject any pytest exit code outside OK and TESTS_FAILED, and made a collection error fatal however pytest chose to exit. Neither guard catches a run that pytest stopped early on purpose.

Verified against the pinned pytest: a suite of three tests where the first fails exits 1 under both -x and --maxfail=1, having run one test of three. That is TESTS_FAILED, which the runner treats as an ordinary suite with failures and profiles happily. (so-2os's own description listed --maxfail under exit 2; that is wrong for this pytest.)

EFFECT: the two tests that never ran have no coverage context, so the optimiser cannot select them and every branch only they reach is counted as uncovered or unattributable. The smoke suite is selected from a profile of part of the suite, and nothing in the output says so -- the same silent under-selection so-2os and so-mr0 were written to eliminate, arriving through a third door.

Users reach it easily: -x or --maxfail=N in --pytest-args, or either one sitting in the project's own addopts where no flag smoke-optimiser sees ever mentions it. addopts is the worse case, because the user need not know the run was truncated at all.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py -- USABLE_EXIT_CODES and the loop in run_profiling; PYTEST_HOOK_CODE, which is where any detection would have to live.

NEEDS A DESIGN DECISION on how to detect truncation without false positives. The obvious signal -- fewer outcomes recorded than items collected -- is not sound as it stands:
  - pytest_collection_modifyitems sees items after deselection, so -k and -m do not inflate the count, but a plugin deselecting later would.
  - A skipped test never reaches the call phase and so is absent from outcomes, and skips are entirely legitimate.
  - Under xdist the collected count is per-worker and would have to be summed the same way outcomes are.
A cleaner signal may be session.shouldstop, or pytest's own testsfailed/maxfail state read in pytest_unconfigure, which says truncation happened rather than inferring it from a count. Whichever is chosen, the run must fail loudly like a collection error does, not warn.

ACCEPTANCE: a project whose suite is truncated by -x or --maxfail (whether from --pytest-args or from addopts) fails loudly rather than producing a smoke suite; a suite that runs to completion with failing tests still profiles as it does today; skipped and deselected tests do not trip the check.

title: Decide whether --smoke and --downwind may be passed to pytest together
description: smoke_optimiser/plugin.py registers --smoke and --downwind as independent boolean flags with independent stashes. pytest_collection_modifyitems runs the smoke filter and then the downwind filter unconditionally when both are set, so passing both flags together silently intersects a coverage-bet selection with a categorical selection -- two answers with different, incompatible promises collapse into whatever tests happen to appear in both files, with no warning that this happened. Neither flag's report header mentions the other being active either, so a user passing both by mistake (e.g. a copy-pasted CI command) gets no signal. Surfaced while implementing so-uom (jr5.4 will be the one wiring --downwind into real invocations, so this should land before or alongside that work). Decide: reject the combination outright (pytest.exit early in pytest_configure), or is intersecting the two selections actually meaningful enough to support and just needs a report-header line making it explicit? No existing test exercises this combination either way.
design:
--smoke and --downwind are mutually exclusive. Passing both makes pytest_configure exit with returncode 1 before either selection file is loaded.

Rationale: the two flags answer different questions with incompatible promises. --smoke is a coverage bet -- a static subset that makes no promise about what it skips. --downwind is categorical -- every test the profile says a change can reach. Applying both filters in sequence yields their intersection, which is neither: not the highest-coverage-per-second subset, and not a complete answer for the change. The epic's governing rule is that the maps must never guess and there is no best-effort middle, so a selection neither mode can justify must be impossible to ask for rather than quietly produced.

The blind-spot path makes it sharper. When a downwind selection has blind spots, _filter_to_downwind_suite deliberately leaves collection untouched because the honest answer is the full suite. Under --smoke the smoke filter has already cut collection down, so the one path that exists specifically to be safe would silently become the least safe one.

Alternatives considered:
- Downwind wins, warn and ignore --smoke. Rejected: silently discarding a flag the user explicitly passed is the same class of problem as the intersection, just quieter.
- Allow the intersection and name it in the report header. Rejected: it legitimises a selection with no statable promise, and still needs a separate fix for the blind-spot fallback.
acceptance_criteria: A decision is recorded (as a design note or ADR-style comment) on whether --smoke and --downwind may coexist, and the plugin's behavior matches it: either pytest.exit's with a clear error when both are passed, or the report header/warnings make an intersected selection explicit rather than silent.
close_reason: Decided: the combination is refused. pytest_configure now exits with a clear error naming both flags and why they conflict, placed above the two loaders so the failure is about the flags rather than whichever selection file happens to be missing. Covered by tests/test_plugin.py::test_plugin_smoke_and_downwind_together_is_refused, which passes a missing smoke path alongside a valid downwind file to pin the guard's position. Full design rationale recorded in the issue's design field.

title: BlindSpotModel and DownwindSuiteFile don't validate their own documented invariants
description: BlindSpotModel's docstring (smoke_optimiser/reports/downwind_suite.py) states 'file is None only for RESOLUTION_ERRORS' and 'resolution_errors is populated only for that same reason', and write_downwind_suite's docstring states 'node_ids is empty whenever blind_spots is non-empty'. None of these are enforced by the pydantic models -- nothing stops constructing BlindSpotModel(reason=UNKNOWN_PATH, file=None) (the plugin's report header would then render 'unknown_path: None'), BlindSpotModel(reason=RESOLUTION_ERRORS, file='some/path.py') with no count, or a DownwindSuiteFile with both a non-empty node_ids and a non-empty blind_spots (the plugin silently ignores node_ids in that case via _filter_to_downwind_suite's early return, with no warning that it was given and dropped). Add pydantic model_validator(s) enforcing: (1) file is set iff reason != RESOLUTION_ERRORS, (2) resolution_errors is set iff reason == RESOLUTION_ERRORS, (3) node_ids and blind_spots are not both non-empty. Surfaced while implementing so-uom; not caught by the tests added there since they only construct well-formed instances.
acceptance_criteria: Constructing a BlindSpotModel with a reason/file/resolution_errors combination that violates the stated invariant raises ValidationError. Constructing a DownwindSuiteFile with both node_ids and blind_spots non-empty raises ValidationError. Existing well-formed construction and round-trip tests in tests/test_downwind_suite.py continue to pass.
close_reason: Added pydantic model_validators to BlindSpotModel (reason/file/resolution_errors consistency) and DownwindSuiteFile (node_ids/blind_spots mutual exclusivity); added tests covering each violation.

title: Version the profile file, so an incompatible profile says so instead of failing as a validation error
description:
ProfilingDataFile (profiler/models.py) carries no schema version. .smoke_suite.json has had one since it was written -- version: int = 1 plus generator_version (reports/smoke_suite.py:53-55) -- but the profile the downwind maps are built from has none.

The gap is already visible in the code. cli.py:115-119 catches a ValidationError while loading .smoke_profiling_data.json and tells the user 'If this profile was recorded by an older version, re-run the profiling phase to regenerate it' -- a diagnosis the data cannot support. The loader has no way to distinguish an old profile from a corrupt one, so it guesses, and the user sees a Pydantic field trace rather than a statement about what is wrong and what to do.

This stops being cosmetic the moment so-n6b.1 lands. so-n6b.14 settled that the profile records the scope roots it was captured under, and that a profile with no recorded scope is a hard error rather than a silent full-suite run. Without a version, 'no recorded scope' is indistinguishable from 'malformed file', and the error cannot name the fix.

REQUIRED, NOT DEFAULTED. .smoke_suite.json uses version: int = 1, which means a file with no version validates as version 1. The profile must not copy that: the field is required with no default, so a pre-versioning profile fails to validate loudly rather than being silently read as the current schema. That is the whole point of adding it.

The loader compares the file's version against the version this build writes and, on a mismatch, exits with a message that names both versions and says to reprofile. It does not attempt migration: this is a 0.x library, a profile is a cache that one instrumented run rebuilds, and migration code for a regenerable artefact is cost without benefit.
acceptance_criteria: ProfilingDataFile carries a required, non-defaulted schema version, written on capture and checked on load. A profile written by an older schema is rejected with a message naming the expected and found versions and telling the user to reprofile -- distinct from the message for a corrupt or unreadable file, and demonstrated by a test for each. cli.py's existing 'recorded by an older version' text is either made true or removed. No migration path. The version bump is noted in CHANGELOG.md as a breaking change.
notes: Blocks so-n6b.1 because n6b.1's hard-error-on-missing-scope behaviour cannot report itself accurately without a version to point at. Without one, 'this profile predates the recorded scope field' and 'this file is corrupt' are the same Pydantic ValidationError.
close_reason: ProfilingDataFile now carries a required, non-defaulted schema_version field (PROFILE_SCHEMA_VERSION=1). load_profiling_data_file checks it before Pydantic validation runs and raises ProfileSchemaMismatchError, which cli.py reports with a distinct message naming both versions and telling the user to reprofile -- separate from the generic 'failed to parse' message used for genuine corruption. The old 'recorded by an older version' guess is removed from the generic message. Noted in CHANGELOG.md as a breaking change. Tests cover both error paths in tests/test_profiler_models.py and tests/test_cli.py.

title: Nothing enforces that ProfilingData.tests keys match their outcome's test_id
description:
ProfilingData.tests is a dict[str, ProfilingOutcome] and ProfilingOutcome carries its own test_id, so a test's identity is stored twice with nothing keeping the two in step (smoke_optimiser/profiler/models.py:105, and ProfilingDataModel at :216).

Consumers have already diverged on which copy they read:
- smoke_optimiser/optimiser/greedy.py:172 uses the DICT KEY
- smoke_optimiser/downwind/maps.py _tests_by_file uses OUTCOME.TEST_ID

If a profile ever carries a mismatched pair, greedy selection and the downwind file -> tests map would disagree about what a test is called, and the downwind map would emit ids the runner cannot pass to pytest -- silently, since neither path validates.

The profile is loaded from JSON, so per the project's own rule ('data loaded from a file must be validated ... it may have been edited in between writing and reading') this is exactly the kind of correspondence ProfilingDataModel should be asserting rather than assuming. Noticed while building the downwind maps for so-n6b.8.

Fix: a model_validator on ProfilingDataModel rejecting any key that differs from its outcome's test_id, plus a test for the rejected case. Consider whether test_id should then be dropped from the outcome, leaving the key as the single source of identity.

title: snapshot() silently drops every edge touching a module with no __file__, such as a namespace package
description:
ImportTracer.snapshot builds `files`, a module-name -> project-path mapping, by
reading `__file__` off every module in sys.modules:

    file_attr = getattr(module, "__file__", None)
    if not file_attr:
        continue

then keeps only edges whose BOTH endpoints are in `files`:

    if edge.importer in files and edge.imported in files and ...

A module with no `__file__` is therefore dropped from the graph entirely, along with
every edge touching it, with no error and nothing counted. Namespace packages are
exactly this case: PEP 420 gives them `__file__ = None`, and any project laid out
without `__init__.py` files consists of them.

It currently fails SAFE rather than silently wrong -- the module is absent from
`files`, so it is absent from `unattributed_modules` too, so a change to it reads as
"no entry in the map" and runs the full suite. But that safety is incidental,
resting on a consumer rule that another issue could reasonably optimise away, and
the loss is invisible either way: a project could be missing a third of its graph
with every number in the profile looking healthy.

NEEDS A DECISION on the fix. A namespace package has no file to attribute an edge
to, but it does have `__path__`, and its submodules have real files; whether the
right answer is to resolve the package to its directory, to drop the edge but count
it beside resolution_errors, or to report the module as unattributed, is not
obvious. Whatever is chosen, the drop must stop being silent.
acceptance_criteria: A profile of a project using PEP 420 namespace packages either records edges for them or reports the loss in a countable field; in no case does the graph drop them while reporting zero errors. Covered by a test with a namespace-package fixture.

title: Record which importer each swallowed edge failure belonged to, so the doubt can be localised
description:
ImportTracer swallows edge-resolution failures into a bare count, because raising
inside __import__ would kill the suite being profiled. A count alone cannot be acted
on: it says some edges are missing without saying which, so a consumer can only
trust the whole graph or refuse the whole graph. Refusing it durably disables
change-based selection as the penalty for a defect that is OURS -- the failures are
our name arithmetic meeting legal Python, deterministic, and persisting until we fix
the tracer.

The failure loses the IMPORTED name, but the IMPORTER is still in hand at the point
of failure: _traced_import reads it from globals["__name__"], and
_traced_import_module from the caller frame it already walks. Recording it localises
the doubt, so selection can add the tests reaching those few modules and stay fast
everywhere else (the rule lives in so-n6b.2).

  - ImportGraph grows failed_importers, the modules whose edge recording failed,
    resolved to project-relative files at snapshot time like every other name.
  - Failures that occur BEFORE the importer can be read -- a globals mapping whose
    .get throws, or sys._getframe(1) raising -- have nothing to localise to. These
    are counted separately as unlocalised failures, and they are what still forces a
    full suite.
  - resolution_errors and error_samples stay as they are, for diagnosis.
  - Under xdist the sets union and the counts sum, like the rest of the graph.

Capturing the importer means reading it BEFORE the arithmetic that fails, so the
recording order in both wrappers changes: resolve the importer into a local, then
compute targets inside the try.
acceptance_criteria: A module whose edge arithmetic raises appears in ImportGraph.failed_importers as a project-relative path, while other modules' edges are unaffected. A failure occurring before the importer name is readable increments the unlocalised counter and adds nothing to failed_importers. Both merge correctly across xdist workers: sets union, counts sum.

title: Use the read map so a changed data file selects its readers instead of the whole suite
description:
so-n6b.3 records which files each test reads and which directories it lists. This
consumes those maps, which turns the blunt rule "a changed non-Python path is a
blind spot, so run everything" into a measured answer.

The rule this replaces is deliberately blunt because it has to be: without a read
map, a changed fixtures/rates.yaml and a changed README.md are the same input --
absent from a Python-execution map -- and only the full suite is safe for both.

THE LADDER, for a changed non-Python path P, where dir is the directory holding it:

  1. P matches the environment carve-out       -> blind spot, full suite
  2. P is in the read map's unattributed set   -> blind spot, full suite
  3. P was present when the profile was taken  -> readers(P) | listers(dir)
  4. P is new                                  -> listers(dir) | readers of the
                                                  files directly in dir

Rule 3 is where absence is allowed to mean "nothing depends on this", licensed by
measurement rather than assumption: the tracer watched every open for the whole
suite, and P was there to be opened. It unions in the listers of P's directory
because no rule reads ChangeKind, and a DELETION changes what a listing returns
even for a file nothing ever opened.

Rule 4 answers a file the map never had the chance to see. It has no measurement of
its own, so it inherits what was measured about its directory. A new fixture beside
fixtures/rates.yaml selects the tests that read fixtures, which is bounded
over-selection rather than a full suite. A new file in a directory nothing ever
read or listed -- docs/, most obviously -- selects nothing, because "nothing here
was ever touched" is itself a measured fact about the directory. The leap is that
listing is the only way a test discovers a file it does not name: a literal path
requires the naming code to have changed, and that change is a Python or data edit
the other relations already answer.

A new non-Python file therefore never forces the full suite. Only the carve-out and
an unattributed read do.

The carve-out is defaults plus a [tool.smoke_optimiser] key, so a project can name
its own environment-defining paths. Extending it can only ever ADD full-suite
runs, which is why it is safe to configure where an ignore list is not: a wrong
entry costs time, not correctness.

The read map may only ever ADD selections for Python files, never justify skipping
one. A C library calling fopen() raises no audit event, so a missing read edge is
undetectable, and the coverage and import relations remain the authority wherever
they have an opinion.

This narrows a stated invariant, and the narrowing must be visible rather than a
side effect of the instrumentation. blind_spots.py currently says every reason
over-selects and never under-selects, so seeing one never means a test was
silently dropped. After this, a non-Python file measured as unread selects nothing
at all, which is the one case where that no longer holds -- so the docstring is
rewritten to state the exception and what licenses it, in the same change that
introduces it.
acceptance_criteria:
A changed fixture that tests read selects exactly those tests. A changed file that
was present at profile time and read by nothing selects nothing, and states that it
was measured as unread. A new file in a directory some test globs selects that
test. A new file in a directory nothing ever read or listed selects nothing. A new
file beside files tests do read selects those tests. A changed file in the read
map's unattributed set runs the full suite. A changed uv.lock, pyproject.toml or
Dockerfile runs the full suite regardless of the maps, as does a path a project
added to the carve-out. Deleting a file nothing opened still selects the tests that
listed its directory. blind_spots.py states the one case where a reason no longer
over-selects.
close_reason: The read map is consumed. A changed non-Python path is now answered by a four-rung ladder in rules.py:_read_answer instead of being an unconditional NON_PYTHON_FILE refusal: environment carve-out refuses; an unattributed read refuses; a file present at profile time selects its readers plus the tests that listed its directory; a new file inherits its directory -- the tests that list it, plus the readers of its siblings. A new non-Python file therefore never forces the full suite. Verified end to end on a purpose-built project: changed fixture 2/5 tests, changed doc 0, new doc 0, new fixture in a globbed directory 4/5, deleted unread file selects exactly the globbing test, uv.lock refuses. blind_spots.py now states the one case where a reason no longer over-selects. .downwind.json bumped to version 2 for the new vocabulary. Carve-out is DEFAULT_ENVIRONMENT_FILES plus a [tool.smoke_optimiser] extra_environment_files key -- additive by name so setting it cannot silently drop the lockfile guard.

title: Capture which files each test reads, so a changed data file is answerable instead of unknown
description:
Change-based selection can answer for a Python file two ways: coverage saw a test
execute it, or the import graph says a test's module depends on it. For a data file
-- a YAML or JSON fixture, a Jinja template, a golden/snapshot file, a .sql
migration -- it has neither relation, so absence from the map carries no
information at all. It means "we never looked", not "nothing reads this", and the
only safe reading of it is a full-suite run.

That is a real cost on real edits: today a README change and a fixture change are
indistinguishable, so both run everything.

This issue makes the relation measurable, in three parts.

READS. sys.addaudithook, one hook for the PEP 578 "open" event. Verified to catch
all three read paths uniformly, with the mode included so reads separate from
writes:

  open ('pyproject.toml', 'r', ...)      <- pathlib.Path.read_text
  open ('pyproject.toml', 'r', ...)      <- builtins.open
  open ('pyproject.toml', None, ...)     <- os.open, which bypasses both wrappers

os.open reports mode None, so its access mode comes from the flags argument
instead. One hook where the import tracer needed three patched mechanisms.

LISTINGS. The same hook takes the "os.listdir" and "os.scandir" events, recording
which DIRECTORIES each test listed. A test that globs fixtures/*.yaml never names
the file it opens, so reads alone cannot answer for a file added after profiling:
it was not there to be read, and its absence would read as "nothing reads this".
The directory a test listed is the relation that does answer for it. os.scandir is
what pathlib.Path.glob, glob.glob and os.walk all go through, so those need no
event of their own -- glob.glob's own event carries a pattern rather than a
directory and is deliberately ignored.

PRESENCE. The tracked non-Python files that existed when the run started, from
git ls-files. This is the read map's denominator: without it, "nothing read this
file" and "this file was not there to be read" are the same observation, and the
first is the whole point of the map. Measured at 33-318 files across the fleet,
0.7-12 KB of JSON.

The directory-level fact -- whether anything in a directory was ever touched --
needs no storage of its own. It is derived from the read and listing maps when the
downwind maps are built, exactly as dependents_of is derived by inverting the
import graph.

ATTRIBUTION is easier than for imports: the profiling hook already knows the active
test node id, so reads and listings are direct file -> tests and directory -> tests
relations with no closure step.

SCOPE: reads only, non-Python project paths only. Writes create no dependency.
Python files have two better relations already and are left to them. Paths outside
the repo root, and .venv/site-packages, __pycache__, tmp dirs, .pytest_cache and
the tool's own artefacts -- the coverage database, the outcomes files, the profile
-- are excluded.

BLIND SPOTS, which must be recorded rather than assumed away:
  - A file READ outside any test context (import time, collection) is recorded as
    UNATTRIBUTED, exactly as ImportGraph.unattributed_modules is. A change to one
    means the map cannot answer -> full suite. Reading it as "no test reads this"
    would be silent under-selection.
  - A LISTING outside any test context is NOT recorded, and this is the one place
    the map deliberately discards an observation. The tree is walked constantly
    under no test context -- pytest's collection walks the test tree, importlib
    scans sys.path entries on every import -- so treating those as dependencies
    would put most of the repository permanently in the full-suite bucket and
    leave the map worthless for the commonest case of all, a new file under
    tests/. The cost is a module-level glob() at import time: files it picks up
    that are added LATER are missed. Files it already read are still safe, because
    reading them raises the unattributed read above.
  - A C library calling fopen() directly raises no audit event. That is a missing
    edge with nothing to detect it, and it is the reason this map may only ever
    ADD selections, never justify skipping a Python file.
  - A conditionally-read file (warm vs cold cache) makes the map run-dependent in a
    way the import graph is not.

Environment-defining files stay a fixed full-suite rule regardless of this map:
uv.lock, pyproject.toml and Dockerfiles change behaviour everywhere while nothing
opens them during the run.

WHERE IT LANDS: files_read and directories_listed per test on ProfilingOutcome,
parallel to files_covered, with unattributed_reads and present_files run-wide on
ProfilingData. That is a change to the shape of the profile, so
PROFILE_SCHEMA_VERSION is bumped and persistence.py writes and reads the new
fields. There is no migration: a profile is a cache one instrumented run rebuilds,
so an older one is reported as a mismatch and the user reprofiles.

Scope here is CAPTURE ONLY. Consuming the map for selection is so-n6b.4.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, do not re-propose:
  - A user-configurable ignore list of test-irrelevant paths. Asserting what can be
    measured; wrong entries under-select silently, and it is a config surface we
    would then want to remove.
  - Wrapping builtins.open and io.open the way the import tracer wraps __import__.
    Misses os.open and anything holding an earlier reference; the audit hook is one
    mechanism that catches all of them.
  - Storing a directory-level "nothing here was opened" set in the profile. It is
    free to derive from the read and listing maps at map-build time, so storing it
    would be a second copy of a fact that can disagree with the first.
acceptance_criteria:
A profile records that a test reading fixtures/x.yaml via open(), Path.read_text()
and os.open() depends on that file, in all three cases. A test that globs a
directory records that directory as listed, whether it globbed via glob.glob,
Path.glob or os.walk. A file read only at collection time is recorded as
unattributed, not as unread; a directory listed only at collection time is recorded
as neither. Writes create no entry. Python files, files under .venv, tmp dirs and
the tool's own artefacts are excluded. The non-Python files present when the run
started are recorded. Verified serial and under xdist, where per-worker maps merge
by union and a read one worker could not attribute is resolved against the merged
attributions, as merge_graphs already does for imports.
close_reason: Capture landed: read_tracer.py records per-test file reads (open/os.listdir/os.scandir audit events) and directory listings, unattributed reads, and a git-derived present_files denominator. PROFILE_SCHEMA_VERSION 2->3. Verified end to end on a purpose-built project, serial and under 4 xdist workers: builtins.open, Path.read_text and os.open all attribute to the right test, a globbing test records its directory, a test that reads nothing stays empty. Tracer overhead measured at ~1.5% on smoke-optimiser's own suite (13.31-13.59s baseline vs 13.52-13.77s), inside run-to-run noise.

title: Localise import-graph failures: always run the tests reaching a module with a failed edge
description:
The import tracer swallows edge-resolution failures and counts them, because raising
inside __import__ would kill the suite being profiled. Every swallowed failure is a
MISSING EDGE, and a missing edge under-selects silently: if the lost edge was
tests/test_billing.py -> billing/rates.py, then editing rates.py does not select
test_billing, the commit goes green, and test_billing was the test that would have
caught the bug.

WHOSE DEFECT IT IS decides the policy. It is ours: the swallowed block does name
arithmetic only, so a failure is resolve_absolute_name or edge_targets meeting legal
Python it mishandles -- an unusual __package__, a namespace package, a module whose
globals lack __name__, an odd fromlist from a third-party caller of __import__. The
project cannot repair it; the error samples are a bug report addressed to us. The
user must not be made to pay a full suite on every commit for that, especially since
the failures are deterministic and will persist until we ship a fix.

LOCALISE THE DOUBT. The failure loses the IMPORTED name while the IMPORTER is still
in hand (so-n6b.5 records it). So the question "does changed file F affect module M"
is unanswerable for those M, and the sound rule is the inverse of a per-file
fallback: selection ALWAYS additionally runs every test whose closure reaches a
module in failed_importers. If three modules had failures, every selection carries
those three modules' dependents, every run, until the tracer is fixed. Bounded,
small, and safe by construction.

UNLOCALISED FAILURES -- where even the importer could not be read -- have nothing to
attach to and do force the full suite. Rare, and counted separately for exactly this
reason.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, do not re-propose:
  - Full suite on any non-zero resolution_errors, matching the time-based
    optimiser's refusal of an xdist profile. Consistent, but it disables the
    feature durably as the penalty for our own bug, and the xdist precedent differs:
    a parallel profile is something the USER chose and can undo.
  - A threshold on the error fraction. The number would be invented, and a single
    missing edge is enough to miss the one test that mattered.
  - Trusting the graph with a warning. That is the silent under-selection this line
    of work exists to prevent, with a warning attached.
  - Treating a change to a failed importer as unanswerable. Wrong direction: the
    lost half is what it imported, so a change to the importer itself is exactly the
    case we can still answer.
acceptance_criteria: Given a graph with failed_importers, every selection includes the tests whose closure reaches those modules, in addition to whatever the changed files select. A graph with unlocalised failures takes the full-suite path and names them as the reason. A graph with neither behaves exactly as it does today. The extra selection is reported, so a persistently degraded graph is visible rather than merely slow.
notes: Narrows the blunt rule so-jr5.2 ships with, where any non-zero resolution_errors makes the whole graph untrustworthy and forces the full suite. That is the safe direction, so this is a refinement: it converts a whole-graph refusal into the localised always-run set described above.

title: Record the scope a profile was captured under, so divergence from the tree can be seen at all
description:
A profile can answer confidently and wrongly. Its downwind maps are a fact about the
codebase as it stood when it was captured, and nothing about a per-file lookup notices
that the codebase has moved on.

Concretely: the profile is captured at commit A. Since then a teammate added
billing/discounts.py and tests/test_discounts.py, and edited billing/rates.py so it now
imports discounts. You edit billing/rates.py. The maps HAVE an entry for it and answer
with the tests that touched it at commit A -- and test_discounts, which now exercises
rates through discounts, is not among them. Nothing tripped the per-change fallback,
because every file you touched was known. Silent under-selection.

EXPIRY IS DIVERGENCE, NOT AGE. A profile is expired once a file exists that its maps
have never seen. That is the observable signature of the codebase having grown past the
map, and it is a fact rather than a threshold: no configured number, no per-project
tuning, nothing to get wrong.

That comparison is only meaningful over files a REGENERATED profile would know about,
so this issue delivers the fact it is read from: the SCOPE a profile was captured under,
resolved by the profiling run itself and recorded into the profile, plus the pure
predicate that applies it. The expiry test is one line over that predicate and lives in
so-jr5.2 with the other rules; so-jr5.4 enumerates the tree and passes it in. Expired
behaves exactly like absent: run the full suite.

THE SCOPE IS RESOLVED INSIDE THE PROFILED PYTEST PROCESS, because that is the only place
a project's own [tool.pytest.ini_options] addopts and testpaths have been applied -- the
process that launched pytest cannot see them, so anything it computed could disagree
with the run that produced the maps. Coverage sources are resolved the way coverage.py
resolves them: a path if one exists, otherwise an importable name, which is what a src
layout needs.

COVERAGE ROOTS AND TEST ROOTS ARE RECORDED SEPARATELY, because they carry different
precision. Coverage records every .py file beneath its roots, executed or not, so all of
them are in scope. A test root is only as precise as the project made it: testpaths =
["tests"] names a directory whose every .py file is test code, support modules included,
while a project that configures nothing leaves pytest pointed at the repository root. In
that one case scope narrows to the files pytest would actually collect, and the run warns
with the steps that fix it -- otherwise a vendored package's suite or a manual
scripts/test_connection.py is permanently unknown and the profile permanently expired.

so-n6b.7 measures how often the cliff is actually crossed. If it turns out to be daily,
this decision gets revisited against a real distribution.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, do not re-propose:

* Wall-clock age past a configured threshold. A heuristic that reads a day of heavy
  refactoring as fresh and an untouched fortnight as stale, while measuring nothing that
  actually breaks the map.
* A divergence threshold ("expired after N new files"). The number would be invented, and
  one new test file is enough to miss the test that mattered.
* Selecting every collected test the profile has never seen, instead of expiring. Cheaper,
  and it does catch new test files -- but it leaves exactly the rates.py case above
  under-selecting, since the stale answer there involves no new test at all.
* One flat set of scope roots, any .py file beneath one in scope. Correct wherever a
  project sets testpaths, and simpler -- but a project that sets none has a test root of
  the repository root, which puts every stray script in scope, unknowable however often
  the profile is regenerated, and pins it to expired forever.
* Applying pytest's collection patterns to every test root. Survives the repository-root
  case, but drops test support modules (tests/helpers/factories.py) that a regenerated
  profile WOULD know, which under-selects silently -- the failure this issue exists to
  prevent, in miniature.
acceptance_criteria:
ProfilingData and the profile file carry the scope the profiling run resolved:
coverage roots, test roots and pytest's collection patterns, all
repository-relative. The schema version is bumped, so a profile without a scope is
rejected as a version mismatch rather than read as one that measured nothing.

files_in_scope() answers which files a regenerated profile would know about: a .py
file under a coverage root, or under a test root -- narrowed, for a test root of the
repository root alone, to what pytest would collect. Demonstrated for a non-Python
file, a .py file outside every root (this repository's scripts/branch_summary.py is
the live example), a test support module under a precise test root, and a stray
script under a repository-root test root.

A profile of the current schema recording no scope at all is a HARD ERROR naming
both the command to run and the settings to check, distinct from the messages for a
corrupt file and a version mismatch, and carrying the schema version so-n6b.16
records.

A run whose test root is the repository root warns, naming the steps that fix it:
create tests/, move the tests there, set testpaths, reprofile.

A profile regenerated against an unchanged tree is NOT expired, demonstrated end to
end: profile a fixture repository, regenerate, and assert every in-scope tracked
file is known to the maps -- including a measured-but-never-imported module and a
test helper -- while its tracked script and data file stay out of scope.
notes:
SCOPE comes from so-n6b.14: the coverage targets and the pytest test paths, resolved at
capture time and recorded in the profile, so 'known to the maps' and 'in scope for
expiry' cannot drift apart. A file in scope is one a freshly regenerated profile would
know.

EXPIRY'S DOMAIN is tracked files you did NOT change -- the pull-or-checkout case, which
is the only one no other rule sees. Files you did change, tracked or not, are so-7hr's
changed set and are answered by so-jr5.2's unknown-changed-path rule. The two domains are
disjoint by construction, so a given file has one reason rather than two.

The expiry TEST lives in so-jr5.2 as 'any(not maps.knows(p) for p in existing_files)', on
the third input so-n6b.11 settled. so-jr5.4 enumerates the tree with 'git ls-files' and
scopes it through files_in_scope(); the rules stay pure and IO-free.

This issue expires on a changed TREE within a fixed scope. Expiring because the SCOPE
itself changed is so-n6b.18: sound in principle, but it needs the effective scope of the
next run to be knowable ahead of that run, which smoke-optimiser cannot currently
determine.
close_reason:
Delivered as the capture-time half of expiry: the profile now records what it measured,
and a pure predicate says which files that covers. The expiry test itself is one line
over that predicate and stays in so-jr5.2, with so-jr5.4 enumerating the tree -- the
issue's acceptance criteria were rewritten to that boundary, since as originally written
they described end-to-end behaviour this issue blocks rather than contains.

WHAT LANDED
* smoke_optimiser/profiler/scope.py: ProfileScope (coverage_roots, test_roots,
  test_file_patterns), resolve_scope() and files_in_scope().
* The scope is resolved INSIDE the profiled pytest process, in the injected hook, from
  pytest-cov's resolved cov_source, pytest's own config.args and config.getini
  ('python_files'). Nothing outside that process can see a project's addopts or
  testpaths, so nothing outside it can state the scope without risking disagreement with
  the run that produced the maps. Coverage sources resolve as coverage.py resolves them:
  path first, then importable name (a src layout needs this), dropped if they land
  outside the repository, kept verbatim if unresolvable rather than failing a finished
  instrumented run.
* PROFILE_SCHEMA_VERSION 1 -> 2 with a required 'scope' field, so a version 1 profile is
  refused as a mismatch. A version 2 profile whose scope names nothing raises
  ProfileScopeMissingError, reported by the CLI with its own message naming both the
  command and the settings to check -- reprofiling alone would not fix that case.
* A capture-time warning, with numbered steps, when the resolved test root is the
  repository root.
* CHANGELOG breaking-change entry; PRD section 5.3 documents the field and the rule.

WHY THE SCOPE IS TWO KINDS OF ROOT RATHER THAN ONE FLAT SET, refining so-n6b.14's flat
rule: a project that configures no testpaths leaves pytest pointed at the repository
root, so under the flat rule every stray tracked .py -- a manual script, a vendored
suite, an example -- is in scope, unknowable however often the profile is regenerated,
and the profile is born expired. Narrowing every test root by pytest's collection
patterns fixes that but drops test support modules (tests/helpers/factories.py) under a
precise root, which a regenerated profile WOULD know, and that under-selects silently.
Coverage roots therefore keep the flat rule, precise test roots keep the flat rule, and
only a test root of the repository root -- where location carries no information at all
-- narrows to what pytest would collect. The narrowing is what the new warning tells
users how to get out of.

VALIDATION: ruff check, ruff format, ty check, 199 tests pass. The end-to-end test
profiles a fixture git repository, regenerates, and asserts not-expired both times over
files_in_scope('git ls-files') -- which also confirms empirically that coverage records
files it never executed, so a measured-but-never-imported module is known rather than
divergent.

title: Give the downwind selection its own file schema and pytest flag
description:
The downwind selection is written to a file that the pytest plugin reads, so pytest
runs the chosen node ids without a command line carrying a full suite's worth of
arguments.

IT IS ITS OWN FILE, WITH ITS OWN SCHEMA AND ITS OWN FLAG: `.downwind.json`, read
under `pytest --downwind`, with `--downwind-file-path` to relocate it. It shares
nothing with
SmokeSuiteFile but the list of node ids. SmokeSuiteFile exists to describe a
coverage bet: SummaryModel requires total_branches, full_suite_branches_covered,
smoke_branches_covered, smoke_coverage_pct and both runtimes; SmokeConfigModel
requires time_cap and target_cov; SelectedTestModel carries duration_s,
branches_covered, marginal_branches and efficiency. A downwind selection has no
time cap, no coverage target and no efficiency ranking, so every one of those fields
would be a zero, and the plugin's report header would announce "0.0% coverage" for a
selection making no coverage claim at all.

THE SCHEMA describes the categorical promise instead: the changed files it was
computed from, the node ids selected, the profile it was computed against, and --
when the answer is the full suite -- which blind spot forced it and why.
The reason is part of the file, not just console output, because it is what the
developer needs when the tool declines to select.

THE PLUGIN gets `--downwind` rather than teaching `--smoke` two meanings. Its report
header and its "test not found in collection" warning both currently assume the
coverage-suite framing and need their own wording here: a selected test missing from
collection means something different when the claim is categorical.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, do not re-propose:
  - One file with a mode discriminator and optional summary blocks. One flag for the
    user, but the schema then describes two unrelated things, every coverage field
    becomes optional, and the plugin branches on mode everywhere anyway.
  - Printing node ids for the caller to pass to pytest, with no file at all. Puts a
    full suite's worth of argv on the command line at 2600 tests, and the full-suite
    fallback must run through our own entry point for the instrumented rewrite to
    happen, so the caller cannot own the pytest invocation.
acceptance_criteria: A written selection file validates against its own model and carries the changed files, the selected node ids, the profile identity, and a reason when the answer is the full suite. The plugin run under its own flag collects exactly the listed node ids. The plugin's report header makes no coverage claim. .smoke_suite.json and the coverage-per-second path are untouched.
close_reason: Implemented in smoke_optimiser/reports/downwind_suite.py: DownwindSuiteFile (own version, changed_files, node_ids, profile identity as commit+timestamp, blind_spots) plus write/read helpers, and wired --downwind/--downwind-file-path into plugin.py with its own filtering, missing-test warning wording, and a coverage-free report header. Confirmed with the user: blind_spots is a list of {reason, file, resolution_errors} entries (not a single reason) since jr5.2 documents multiple independent rules firing per changed file; BlindSpotReason enum values are fixed now (unknown_path, non_python_file, unattributed_import, expired_profile, changed_conftest, resolution_errors) rather than left as free text; node_ids is left empty when blind_spots is non-empty because the only reader is the plugin, whose fallback behaviour is 'don't filter' -- pytest already collects everything for free, so enumerating every id would add nothing for either the plugin or a human reading the file. .smoke_suite.json and the coverage-per-second path are untouched.

title: Collect the changed-file set from git: staged, unstaged and untracked, with renames and deletions
description:
Downwind selection needs the set of files that have changed, expressed the same way
the profile expresses paths.

THE CHANGED SET is the union of staged, unstaged and untracked changes. pytest reads
the WORKTREE, not the index, so a selection made from the index alone would run
tests against code the index does not contain -- testing something other than what
was measured. Untracked files are included: a brand new module has no map entry, so
it lands in the full-suite fallback, which is the right answer and only reachable if
the file is seen at all.

RENAMES are detected with -M and resolved to the OLD path. That is the only path the
profile knows, and a pure move is the common case; the alternative makes every
rename cost a full suite for nothing.

DELETIONS are looked up in the map exactly like any other change. The tests that
executed a deleted file are precisely the ones most likely to break, so nothing in
this path may gate on whether a path still exists on disk.

PATHS are repo-relative (so-746 makes the profile's paths repo-relative too), so the
two sides agree by construction.

Returns a typed result, not a bare list of strings: each entry carries its path and
its change kind, since the downwind rules treat a deletion, a rename and an addition
differently.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, do not re-propose:
  - Staged-only (git diff --cached), the obvious precommit choice. Rejected because
    pytest runs against the worktree.
  - Forgoing -M so a rename arrives as an add plus a delete. Correct but wasteful:
    the add is unknown, which forces a full suite on every move.
  - Taking the file list as an argument and doing no git work here. Rejected: the
    tool owns the promise, so it must own the definition of what it is promising
    about.
acceptance_criteria: A file edited but not staged appears in the set. An untracked file appears. A renamed file appears once, as its OLD path. A deleted file appears and is never filtered out for not existing. Every path is repo-relative regardless of the directory the command ran from. Each entry carries its change kind.
close_reason: Implemented changed_files(repo_root) in smoke_optimiser/downwind/changes.py, parsing git status --porcelain=v2 -z (staged+unstaged+untracked union, -M renames resolved to old path, deletions never filtered). Design decisions confirmed with user: repo_root is a caller-supplied parameter (not self-discovered), missing/failed git raises GitStatusError, and edge statuses (merge conflicts, type changes) classify as MODIFIED. 15 new tests in tests/test_downwind_changes.py against real temp git repos; 95% branch coverage on the new module.

title: A missing import graph file is indistinguishable from a graph with no edges
description:
_read_iteration_graph (smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py) globs the temp directory for graph files, reads what it finds, and merges them:

    paths = sorted(import_graph_json.parent.glob(...))
    graphs = [read_graph(path) for path in paths]
    return merge_graphs(graphs)

With NO files present that is merge_graphs([]), which returns a perfectly valid
ImportGraph with no edges, no unattributed modules and no errors. Nothing raises.

WHY THAT IS DANGEROUS. An empty graph does not read as 'unknown', it reads as
'nothing in this project imports anything'. Every file then looks like a file no
module depends on, so change-based selection (so-jr5.2) would select no tests for a
change to any of them -- the silent under-selection this whole line of work
exists to prevent. Contrast the sibling path: _read_iteration_outcomes raises
OutcomesIngestError on an unreadable file, and a malformed graph raises
ImportGraphIngestError. Only ABSENCE is silent.

WHEN IT HAPPENS. pytest_unconfigure writes the graph, and it does not run if the
process is hard-killed (timeout, OOM, SIGKILL) -- see so-fp4 for the same class
of problem in the coverage database. Under xdist it is worse and more likely: one
killed worker means one missing file, so the merged graph silently lacks that
worker's edges while looking complete.

NEEDS A DESIGN DECISION. The runner knows how many graph files it should expect
in the serial case (exactly one), but under xdist it only learns the worker count
from the outcomes files it reads in the same iteration. Options: require at least
one graph file per iteration and error otherwise; cross-check the graph file count
against the worker count the outcomes reported; or have the hook write a sentinel
early so absence is detectable. Whatever is chosen, absence must not be silent.
close_reason:
Fixed in 0210cbe. The three artefacts one iteration leaves behind -- outcomes, import graph, read map -- are counted before they are read, and disagreeing counts are fatal. The expected count is the largest of the three rather than the outcomes count as the issue proposed: the hook writes the graph before the outcomes, so a process killed inside pytest_unconfigure is likelier to leave a graph with no outcomes than an outcomes file with no graph, and anchoring on outcomes would have missed that direction entirely. Under xdist this catches one dead worker, not just a wholly absent graph.

The check runs after the exit code is inspected rather than inside the readers. run_profiling deliberately tolerates a later iteration that pytest reported as fatal -- it is dropped whole and the earlier iterations' coverage stands -- and failing on its missing files inside the reader would have removed that. A killed iteration's absent artefacts are explained by its exit code; only a clean pytest exit with artefacts missing is the silent case this issue is about.

Wider than the issue as written: the read map got the same treatment, since an empty map reads as 'no test opened this file' exactly as an empty graph reads as 'nothing imports this module'. Agreed with the user before implementing.

The mocked subprocess.run in the runner tests now writes what a finished pytest leaves behind and writes nothing when it is killed, which makes the existing later-iteration tolerance test exercise the ordering above rather than pass by accident.

title: CLI boolean defaults silently clobber the same setting from pyproject.toml
description:
resolve_config (smoke_optimiser/config.py) applies a CLI override whenever the value 'is not None'. Typer boolean flags default to False, not None, so they are ALWAYS applied.

Concretely: a project with

  [tool.smoke_optimiser]
  allow_ordered = true

still gets allow_ordered=False on every run that does not pass --allow-ordered, because the CLI's default False overrides it. The setting is silently inert -- the user sees the pytest-randomly error they configured away.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/cli.py builds cli_overrides with 'allow_ordered': allow_ordered; smoke_optimiser/config.py resolve_config's 'value is not None' loop.

The new --allow-parallel-durations flag (so-u3i) deliberately avoids this by passing 'allow_parallel_durations or None', which is the shape every boolean flag should use -- or resolve_config should learn which keys are booleans whose False means 'unset'. Pick one and apply it consistently.

NOT a theory: verified by reading the resolution loop, and the reason the new flag was written differently from its neighbour.
close_reason: Fixed by making boolean CLI flags tri-state: 'bool | None = None' with paired --x/--no-x forms, chosen over the 'flag or None' shape so-u3i used. The issue offered that alternative, but it only fixes precedence in one direction -- a pyproject 'allow_ordered = true' would have become impossible to turn off from the command line. The rule this establishes for so-jr5.4: the CLI wins over pyproject.toml both ways, and 'not passed' is None. Also emits both halves in reports/repro.py, and widened the --help scrape in test_repro_command_completeness_against_help, which the longer paired flag name made wrap and truncate.

title: Fix lint errors after switching ruff to select=ALL
description: pyproject now selects ALL ruff rules; 55 errors across source, scripts and tests need fixing without editing lint rules.
close_reason: Fixed in 53a031d

title: A changed conftest.py puts every test at or below its directory downwind
description:
conftest.py is never imported by test modules -- pytest loads it itself -- so it has no edge in the import graph so-aeo captures, and its fixtures leave no distinguishing mark in files_covered either. Downwind selection would therefore see a changed conftest.py as affecting nothing, which UNDER-selects: silently skipping tests whose fixtures just changed is the worst failure this tool can have.

pytest's own rule is directory scope: a conftest.py applies to every test collected at or below the directory containing it. Mirror exactly that rule.
design:
Replace the CHANGED_CONFTEST blind spot in _blind_spot_reason with a selection, using the directory-scope machinery so-n6b.29 landed: _conftest_directory(path) in downwind/rules.py gives the directory a conftest governs (WHOLE_REPOSITORY for a root conftest), and DownwindMaps.tests_at_or_below(directory) turns that into node ids off the profile's node ids. A repository-root conftest.py therefore selects the whole suite, which is correct.

Read off the node ids rather than coverage on purpose: whether a conftest appears in any files_covered depends entirely on the profiling run's --cov target, and under --cov=mypackage it appears in none.

The rule fires unconditionally for a CHANGED conftest, unlike so-n6b.29's fallback for a conftest that merely sits on the closure's path. That one fires only where both relations answer empty, because coverage names the exact tests that ran a fixture's body and directory scope would throw that precision away. A changed conftest has no such precise answer available: its collection-time code, its hooks and its unused fixtures all affect tests coverage never ties to it.

DELIBERATELY OUT OF SCOPE -- these are separate, harder problems and must NOT be attempted here:

* pytest_plugins declarations, which can load a conftest from an unrelated directory and break the directory-scope assumption.
* Plugins supplied via -p on the command line.
* Fixture-level granularity (working out WHICH fixtures a test actually used).

If the implementation starts needing any of these, stop and re-scope the issue rather than guessing.
acceptance_criteria: A changed tests/sub/conftest.py selects every test under tests/sub/ and no test outside it. A changed conftest.py at the project root selects the entire suite. A changed conftest.py selects those tests even though no test module imports it and it contributes nothing to files_covered.
notes: Narrows the blunt rule so-jr5.2 ships with, where any changed conftest.py is a blind spot and runs the full suite. That rule over-selects rather than under-selects, so this is a refinement of a sound answer, not a fix for a broken one.

title: The 'unattributable coverage context' error asserts a single cause it cannot verify
description:
_verify_contexts (smoke_optimiser/profiler/coverage_db.py:245-252) raises with a message
that names one cause it cannot verify:

  "This usually means the coverage database is stale, or was combined across different
   runs; remove it and profile again."

Three known conditions produce that same symptom -- a coverage context whose test id has
no outcome -- and the message describes only the third:

  - A test process killed outright mid-phase: pytest-timeout sending SIGKILL/SIGTERM, an
    OOM kill, or a segfaulting C extension under test. coverage.py may already have
    flushed a context row for what ran before the kill, but
    pytest_runtest_makereport never fires for that node id, so nothing records an
    outcome. (This is the case so-pc5 did not cover: its fix records an outcome whenever
    makereport fires for a failed setup/teardown phase, which presumes the hook runs at
    all.)
  - An abandoned iteration under --iterations > 1. so-2os keeps the iterations that
    completed and drops the abandoned one's outcomes whole, while its coverage stays in
    the shared database. Ordinarily safe, since the abandoned iteration's contexts are a
    subset of a completed one's -- but a suite whose node ids are not stable between
    iterations (dynamic or randomised parametrisation) leaves a context with no outcome.
  - A genuinely stale or combined database.

The advice is actively wrong for the first two. Removing the database and re-profiling
reproduces the failure whenever the kill is deterministic, which a real timeout is.

The fix here is the message alone: state the symptom, list the causes it could be, and
stop asserting one of them. Telling the three apart from the database side is a separate
question -- see so-fp4's successor issue -- and this does not depend on it.

Raising is the right behaviour and stays: unattributable coverage would silently shrink
the smoke suite, so the run must stop. Only the diagnosis is wrong.

This becomes user-facing on an ordinary command once so-jr5.3 lands: a full-suite
fallback then runs instrumented during a routine downwind run, so a project using
pytest-timeout meets this message without having asked to profile anything.
acceptance_criteria: The error names the symptom and the conditions that can cause it, without asserting one. It no longer advises removing the database as though that were the fix. A test asserts the wording, since nothing does today.

comments.author: lawther
comments.text: so-2os adds a third cause of this same symptom. When --iterations > 1 and a later iteration does not finish, the runner now keeps the iterations that completed and drops the abandoned one's outcomes whole, while its coverage stays in the shared database. In the ordinary case that is safe -- the abandoned iteration's contexts are a subset of a completed one's -- but a suite whose node ids are not stable between iterations (dynamic or randomised parametrisation) can leave a context with no outcome, and _verify_contexts will again blame a stale database. Another reason the message should stop asserting one cause it cannot verify.

title: Multi-iteration duration averaging blends setup-phase duration from a differently-outcomed iteration
description:
Introduced by the so-pc5 fix (runner.py PYTEST_HOOK_CODE now also records failed setup/teardown reports).

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py, the iterations loop around lines 169-178:
  for nodeid, data in raw_outcomes.items():
      all_durations[nodeid].append(data['duration'])
      final_outcomes[nodeid] = data['passed']   # last iteration wins
      final_markers[nodeid] = frozenset(data['markers'])
avg_durations is then sum(all_durations[nodeid]) / len(...) across ALL iterations, unconditionally.

PROBLEM. With config.iterations > 1 and a flaky test whose fixture sometimes errors in setup:
  iteration 1: fixture errors in setup after doing 2.0s of work -> recorded passed=False, duration=2.0 (the setup phase duration)
  iteration 2: fixture succeeds, call passes in 0.01s -> recorded passed=True, duration=0.01
final_outcomes lands on passed=True (last iteration), but avg_durations averages 2.0 and 0.01 together (~1.0s) -- a passing test now reports a duration wildly inflated by an unrelated failing iteration's setup-phase timing.

Before so-pc5, failed iterations were absent from raw_outcomes entirely (the hook only recorded 'call'), so this contamination could not happen -- durations from failing iterations simply were not collected. so-pc5 fixed a real crash but reopened this averaging correctness gap as a side effect.

NEEDS A DESIGN DECISION: should durations only be averaged across iterations whose outcome matches final_outcomes (i.e. only average the 'passed' iterations' durations when the test ultimately counts as passed)? Or bucket durations by outcome and report the one matching final_outcomes? Or something else? This wasn't decided as part of so-pc5 since it's a distinct pre-existing averaging mechanism the fix newly interacts with.

title: Profiling ignores the project's own coverage config, inflating total_branches
description:
runner.py writes its own minimal rcfile and passes it as --cov-config, which
REPLACES the project's coverage configuration rather than extending it:

    COVERAGERC_CONTENT = '''
    [run]
    branch = True
    '''

So the project's own settings are silently discarded during profiling. Most
consequential is [report] exclude_lines. This repository's own pyproject.toml
has:

    exclude_lines = ['pragma: no cover', 'if TYPE_CHECKING:',
                     'def __repr__', 'raise NotImplementedError']

None of these apply while profiling. Branches the project has explicitly
declared un-coverable are therefore counted in total_branches, inflating the
denominator and depressing every reported coverage percentage. [run] omit and
[run] source are dropped for the same reason.

PRE-EXISTING, NOT A so-mr0 REGRESSION -- the old JSON path passed the same
rcfile to 'coverage json', so behaviour is unchanged. It is more VISIBLE now:
so-mr0 computes the denominator in-process from FileReporter using this rcfile,
so the exclusions are absent from both numerator and denominator, and
coverage_db is where the effect now lands.

INTERACTION WITH --target-cov: an inflated denominator makes a given
--target-cov harder to reach than the user intends, and can make a threshold
they set from 'coverage report' output unreachable.

DESIGN DECISION. Merging user config is not free: an omit or source setting that
conflicts with --src, or a dynamic_context already set to something other than
'test', would break profiling. Options are to layer our [run] settings over the
discovered config, or to read only [report] exclusions, or to keep replacing but
warn when the project has settings we are discarding.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py COVERAGERC_CONTENT; consumed by
smoke_optimiser/profiler/coverage_db.py::read_coverage_db via config_file.

ACCEPTANCE: a branch marked 'pragma: no cover' does not appear in
total_branches, and profiling still works for a project with no coverage
configuration at all.
notes:
The dropped [run] source now costs more than measurement fidelity. The profile records
the scope it was captured under (smoke_optimiser/profiler/scope.py), and that scope is
read off the --cov flags pytest-cov resolved -- so a project that declares its coverage
source only in [tool.coverage.run] gets neither the measurement it asked for nor a
recorded scope matching its layout. Whatever replaces COVERAGERC_CONTENT should therefore
keep the two in step: the scope must stay a description of what was actually measured,
which is the property that lets a profile say it has gone stale.

title: pytest's exit code is ignored, so a collection error silently yields a partial smoke suite
description:
runner.py runs the suite with check=False and never inspects the return code:

    subprocess.run(pytest_cmd, cwd=project_root, check=False, env=env)

Exit code 1 (tests failed) is expected and correctly handled -- failing tests are
hard-excluded. But every other non-zero code is swallowed:

  2  interrupted (e.g. Ctrl-C, or --maxfail reached)
  3  internal error
  4  usage error (e.g. a bad --pytest-args value)
  5  no tests collected

A COLLECTION ERROR IN ONE FILE is the dangerous case. pytest still runs and
still writes coverage for everything it did collect, so profiling proceeds
happily and emits a smoke suite that is simply missing every test in the broken
file. The user gets a green-looking result that under-selects, with no
indication anything was skipped. That is precisely the silent under-selection
so-mr0 was written to eliminate -- so-mr0 closed the ingest hole but this one is
upstream of it and still open.

Exit 5 (no tests collected) is currently caught downstream by chance: no
coverage database means CoverageIngestError. The message will talk about a
missing database rather than about no tests being collected.

DECISION NEEDED on --iterations > 1: if iteration 3 of 5 is interrupted, is the
accumulated coverage still usable, or is the whole run void? Coverage
accumulates across iterations into one database, so a partial iteration
contributes real data but skews nothing except durations.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py:157

ACCEPTANCE: a project with one uncollectable test file fails loudly rather than
producing a smoke suite; exit code 1 still proceeds as it does today.
close_reason:
Two signals now guard the profiling run, because the exit code alone cannot carry it.

The inline profiling hook grows a pytest_collectreport hook that records every node id pytest failed to collect, merged across xdist workers through the outcomes file (OutcomesFileModel gains a required collection_errors list). Any collection error is fatal however many iterations have already run: the same files fail to collect every time, so accumulated coverage never makes up for tests that were never collected. This is what closes the hole the issue was aimed at -- --continue-on-collection-errors makes a collection error exit 1, indistinguishable from ordinary test failures, and a project can set it in its own addopts where no flag smoke-optimiser sees ever mentions it.

The exit code is then checked against pytest.ExitCode: OK and TESTS_FAILED proceed, everything else (plus codes pytest does not define, e.g. a signal) is fatal, each with its own message -- NO_TESTS_COLLECTED now says so instead of falling through to a missing-database CoverageIngestError.

Decision on --iterations > 1: an abandoned iteration stops the loop but keeps what completed. Coverage accumulates into one database, so the earlier iterations' work is intact; the abandoned iteration's outcomes and import graph are dropped whole, since tests it never reached would be averaged over fewer samples than the rest. If the first iteration is the one that fails there is nothing to keep, and the run fails.

Tests: three e2e runs over a project with one uncollectable test file (default exit 2, --continue-on-collection-errors exit 1, and a plain failing test that must still profile), plus unit coverage of each fatal exit code, the mid-run abandonment, and the hook recording collection errors.

title: README: prefer config over CLI for stable pytest args, and warm the profile in new worktrees
description:
Two small README gaps that each cost an adopter a cycle.

CONFIG OVER CLI FOR STABLE ARGUMENTS. The one project running downwind in anger passes -n auto --dist=worksteal through --pytest-args on the command line. downwind_pytest_args already exists as a config key and is the better home for anything stable: it is what lets a shared, synced justfile recipe stay byte-identical across several repos while each tunes itself. The table documents both without saying which to reach for. A line -- config for what does not change, CLI for one-offs -- is all it needs, and it is what makes a fleet-wide shared recipe possible at all.

WORKTREES PAY A FULL SUITE EACH. The profile is gitignored and per-checkout, so every new git worktree pays one instrumented full suite on its first commit. For a project whose suite needs Docker and testcontainers that is a surprising first commit in a fresh worktree. A line recommending `smoke-optimiser smoke --profile-only` as a worktree-setup step covers it.

Sharing one profile across worktrees of the same repo is arguably sound -- they are the same path space -- but that is a design question, not a doc fix, and is deliberately not proposed here.
acceptance_criteria: The README says which of --pytest-args and downwind_pytest_args to reach for and why, and tells worktree users to pre-warm the profile.

title: include_namespace_packages is read via pytest-cov's private _cov plugin attributes, with a silent fallback
description:
so-n6b.50's fix reads the profiled run's real include_namespace_packages setting from smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py's pytest_unconfigure hook via:

    config.pluginmanager.get_plugin('_cov').cov_controller.cov.config.include_namespace_packages

'_cov' and cov_controller are pytest-cov's internal plugin registration name and attribute, not part of its public API (confirmed by reading pytest_cov/plugin.py -- CovPlugin registers itself under '_cov' and exposes cov_controller.cov as the underlying coverage.Coverage object). A pytest-cov internal refactor could rename or remove either without a deprecation, and the current code has no test pinned to a pytest-cov version to catch that.

The failure mode is silent and safe-by-default: getattr(..., None) chains mean any breakage just yields include_namespace_packages=False, the conservative choice (package-walk restriction stays on) -- so this would not misclassify a project that has actually turned the setting on; it would just silently stop reading it. Still worth either finding a public pytest-cov API for this, or adding a version-compat test/comment that fails loudly if pytest-cov's internal shape changes.

title: The 'regenerate it' hint ignores a profile path given on the command line
description:
REGENERATE_COMMAND (smoke_optimiser/downwind/command.py:67) is a literal:

    REGENERATE_COMMAND = "smoke-optimiser smoke --profile-only"

It is printed in the two places downwind says the profile is the problem (command.py:202
and :307), and it ignores the configuration of the run that printed it. A user who ran
'downwind --profile-path build/profile.json' is told to run a command that writes to
.smoke_profiling_data.json instead, so following the advice exactly leaves downwind still
unable to find a profile, with no hint as to why. The path resolved from
[tool.smoke_optimiser] in pyproject.toml is safe, since the suggested command reads the
same table -- only a path given on downwind's own command line goes wrong.

This is the pattern build_repro_command (smoke_optimiser/reports/repro.py) already exists
to get right: it renders --profile-path from the resolved config rather than assuming the
default. The suggestion here should be built the same way, from the DownwindConfig the
command already holds.

Also worth settling while here: --profile-only is no longer what distinguishes a run that
records a profile, since so-n6b.25 made every smoke run write one. The flag is still the
cheapest way to record a profile without also building a smoke suite, so it is probably
still the right thing to suggest -- but that is now a choice rather than the only option,
and it should be a deliberate one.
