acceptance_criteria: The suggested command names the profile path the run was actually configured with, so running it verbatim produces a profile the same downwind invocation then finds.

title: downwind pads the changed-file list with the tool's own artefacts: the smoke suite file and a killed run's .tmp
description:
changed_files runs `git status --untracked-files=all`, so files this tool wrote itself
appear in the changed set on any project that has not gitignored them. The developer reads
their own change buried in a list naming our artefacts:

    🎯 1 of 1 tests downwind of 7 changed files.
         .smoke_profiling_data.json.tmp
         .smoke_suite.json
         src/__pycache__/app.cpython-312.pyc
         ...
         src/app.py

The selection is correct -- the read map answers "nothing read these" and they contribute
no tests and no blind spot -- so this is legibility, not correctness. It is worth fixing
because the changed-file list is the tool's account of WHY it selected what it did, and an
account padded with the tool's own leavings is one a developer stops reading.

`_drop_own_artefacts` in downwind/command.py already excludes the paths downwind resolves:
the profile (`--profile-path`), the `.corrupt` copy a fallback leaves behind, and the
selection file (`--downwind-file-path`). TWO PATHS REMAIN:

1. THE SMOKE SUITE (`--output-json`, default `.smoke_suite.json`). Not merely missing from
   the exclusion set -- it is not a field on DownwindConfig at all, because downwind never
   reads it. Excluding it means downwind resolving a setting that belongs to the other
   command, which is the thing DownwindConfig was deliberately shaped to avoid. That is the
   decision this issue turns on.
2. A KILLED RUN LEAVING `.smoke_profiling_data.json.tmp`. save_profile stages the write
   beside the target so a kill cannot destroy the previous profile (so-n6b.46), and no
   cleanup can run when the process is killed outright. The right trade for the profile,
   but it leaves a path behind that nothing removes. Unlike the smoke suite this one is
   derivable from profile_path without any new configuration, exactly as the `.corrupt`
   sibling is.

WHAT TO DECIDE. For the `.tmp` path, whether to exclude it or to sweep strays at startup,
which also stops them accumulating. For the smoke suite, whether downwind resolves
output_json purely to ignore it, or whether the list instead stays honest and the tool says
nothing -- excluding is the better reading but silently drops a path the user may have
pointed at something real via `--output-json`.

Alternatives considered: a user-configurable ignore list, which the epic rejected. Nothing
here is configurable, and it covers only files this tool produced, which is what makes it a
different proposal rather than that one returning.
acceptance_criteria: A project that has not gitignored the smoke suite sees a changed-file list containing only its own files, and a run killed part-way leaves nothing behind that later runs report as changed. The tool never names a file it wrote itself as an input to its own decision.

comments.author: lawther
comments.text:
Measured today on a fixture repo with no .gitignore: a full 'smoke' run followed by a touched .smoke_profiling_data.json.tmp put both artefacts in the changed set -- 7 changed files -- and downwind still selected '1 of 1 tests downwind'. No blind spot, no full suite.

So the premise 'each is a non-Python file, so each raises a blind spot and the run refuses' is no longer true; the read map answers for both paths with nothing, because nothing read them and nothing listed the root. The 'WHY IT MATTERS' paragraph is out of date with it: the ordinary first-time path of smoke-then-downwind does not lose its selection.

What survives is the tidiness argument -- the tool naming its own files in the developer's changed-file list -- and the design question the body frames well: excluding .smoke_suite.json means downwind resolving a setting belonging to the other command, while the .tmp sibling is derivable from profile_path exactly as .corrupt is. If that is the live work, the body should be rewritten to argue it on those terms rather than on a refusal that no longer happens.

title: Tell a killed test apart from a stale coverage database, rather than describing both
description:
_verify_contexts (smoke_optimiser/profiler/coverage_db.py) finds a coverage context whose
test id has no outcome, and stops the run. That is right -- unattributable coverage would
silently shrink the smoke suite -- but it cannot say which of three conditions it is
looking at, and each wants a different response from the developer:

  - A test process killed outright mid-phase (pytest-timeout, OOM, a segfaulting C
    extension). Re-profiling reproduces it whenever the kill is deterministic. The
    developer needs to know which test died, not to be sent back to profile again.
  - An abandoned iteration under --iterations > 1 whose node ids were not stable between
    iterations. Harmless in itself; the completed iterations are intact.
  - A genuinely stale or combined coverage database, where removing it really is the fix.

so-fp4 makes the message stop asserting one of these. Telling them apart is what is left.

WHAT IS AVAILABLE. The profiling hook knows which node ids pytest started and never
finished a report for, which distinguishes a kill from a stale database without inspecting
the database at all -- a stale row names a test this run never began. The iteration case
is already known to the runner, which chose to drop that iteration's outcomes. Neither
signal reaches coverage_db today.

OPEN QUESTIONS. Whether the hook should record a started-but-unreported node id at all,
given that the process it would record from is the one being killed; whether the runner
should pass what it dropped down to ingestion rather than have ingestion infer it; and
whether a kill should be fatal at all, or should instead exclude that test and its
contexts and carry on with a warning naming it.

This blocks nothing. The run already stops safely in every case.
acceptance_criteria: A hard-killed test is reported as a killed test, naming it. A stale or combined database is still reported as such. A context left by an abandoned iteration is distinguished from both. Whether a kill remains fatal is settled and stated.

title: The profiler reaches into downwind for tracked_files, inverting the dependency between them
description:
profiler/runner.py now imports GitStatusError and tracked_files from downwind/changes.py, to record the present_files denominator the read map is read against. Every other edge between these packages runs the other way: downwind reads the profile the profiler writes.

It is not a cycle -- changes.py imports nothing from the profiler -- so nothing is broken. But the module docstring in changes.py frames it as the other half of what DOWNWIND SELECTION asks of git, and it now has a second caller with a different job, which makes the docstring wrong as well as the layering.

tracked_files and repository_root are git plumbing rather than downwind policy: they shell out to git, they normalise paths to repository-relative posix, and both packages want exactly that. The fix is to move that plumbing somewhere both can depend on without either owning it, and to rewrite the docstrings so each says what it is rather than who happened to ask for it first.

Small and mechanical, but worth doing before a third caller appears and the inversion is load-bearing.

title: Measure how often an unattributed read forces the full suite, since that is the read map's main leak
description:
A file read outside any test -- at import or during collection -- is recorded in ReadObservations.unattributed_reads, and a change to one refuses with UNATTRIBUTED_READ and runs everything. That is the safe reading: something depends on the file and no test can be named.

What is unknown is how big that set is on real projects. On the purpose-built demo it was empty, but that suite reads nothing at import time. A project whose settings module does yaml.safe_load('config/settings.yaml') at import puts that file in the set permanently, and every edit to it runs the whole suite -- exactly the outcome the read map was built to avoid.

If the set turns out to be large across the fleet, the read map buys much less than it appears to and the follow-up is localisation in the shape of so-n6b.2: attribute an import-time read to the tests whose modules transitively import the reader, rather than refusing for the whole suite. The import graph already holds that relation, so the ingredients are present. If the set is small, this is not worth building.

MEASURE: profile casey_ai, enphase_curtailer and fomo, then report per project the size of unattributed_reads, how many of those paths are tracked non-Python files a developer would plausibly edit (excluding pyproject.toml and friends, which the environment carve-out refuses anyway), and what fraction of the tracked non-Python tree that comes to. Gate the localisation work on the answer, exactly as so-n6b.17 is gated on so-n6b.7.

title: A module-level glob at import time makes files later added to that directory invisible
description:
The read tracer records directory listings only while a test is active, and DISCARDS listings made outside any test (read_tracer.py, _record_listing). That is deliberate and load-bearing: pytest's collection walks the test tree and importlib scans every sys.path entry on every import, so recording those would mark most of the repository as depended on and put it permanently in the full-suite bucket -- worthless for the commonest case of all, a new file under tests/.

The cost is a module that globs at IMPORT time:

    RATES = {p.stem: load(p) for p in Path('fixtures').glob('*.yaml')}

The listing happens under no test context and is thrown away. Existing files the glob reads are still safe, because reading them lands in unattributed_reads and refuses. But a file ADDED to that directory afterwards has no read record and no listing record, so downwind rule 4 asks what was measured about the directory, finds the sibling readers -- and those reads were themselves unattributed, so the directory looks untouched and the new file selects NOTHING.

Silent under-selection, though a narrow one: it needs a module-level glob AND a file added to that directory afterwards.

Possible fix, narrower than the rule that was rejected for the general case: record unattributed listings separately rather than discarding them, and consult them ONLY for a file that is new. An unattributed listing would then make a new file in that directory a blind spot, while leaving every changed existing file answered exactly as it is now -- so pytest's collection walk of tests/ costs nothing until someone adds a file there. Whether that trade is worth the extra state needs deciding, not assuming.

Documented as an accepted hole in read_tracer's module docstring and in so-n6b.3; this issue exists so the hole is tracked rather than only described.

title: generator_version is a hardcoded literal, and it has already gone stale
description:
Both output schemas record which build produced them, and both record it as a string literal
that nobody updates:

  smoke_optimiser/reports/smoke_suite.py:55   generator_version: str = '0.1.0'
  smoke_optimiser/reports/downwind_suite.py   generator_version: str = '0.1.0'

The package is at 0.2.0 (pyproject.toml:7), and pytest's own header already reports
'smoke-optimiser-0.2.0' from the installed metadata. So every .smoke_suite.json and
.downwind.json written since the 0.2.0 release claims to have been generated by 0.1.0.

The field exists so a stale or surprising output can be traced to the build that wrote it,
which is precisely what it cannot now do. A wrong version is worse than no version: it sends
whoever is debugging to the wrong changelog.

FIX: read it once from importlib.metadata.version('smoke-optimiser') rather than restating it,
so it cannot drift again. Release-please bumps pyproject.toml and would otherwise have to know
to bump these two literals as well.

Note that downwind_suite.py inherited the literal by being modelled on smoke_suite.py, which is
how a stale default propagates -- worth fixing both together rather than one at a time.

title: Blind spots are rendered by two independent describers, in the command and in the plugin
description:
The same vocabulary is turned into English twice, by two functions that do not know about
each other:

* smoke_optimiser/downwind/command.py _describe() -- one explanatory line per blind spot,
  printed by the command before it runs pytest, saying what would make each input
  answerable.
* smoke_optimiser/plugin.py _describe_blind_spot() -- a terse 'reason: file' clause,
  comma-joined into pytest's report header.

The two audiences are genuinely different, so this is not simply duplication: a report
header cannot carry six explanatory sentences, and the command's output would be useless
if it only named enum values. But a reason added to BlindSpotReason must currently be
handled in both, and only one of them will fail loudly if it is not -- command.py's
_EXPLANATIONS dict raises KeyError, while the plugin's fallthrough silently prints the
raw enum value.

The epic requires the concept to keep its name in every layer. It should probably also
keep its WORDS in every layer: one short form and one long form, both defined beside
BlindSpotReason in blind_spots.py, so adding a reason is one edit that both renderers
pick up.

comments.author: lawther
comments.text: Grew on 2026-09-08 with the read map. Both describers now carry three cases, not two: command.py:_describe and plugin.py:_describe_blind_spot each special-case RESOLUTION_ERRORS and READ_ERRORS before falling through to the per-file form, because both name a count instead of a file. The new blind_spots.WHOLE_MAP_REASONS names that set once, so a third such reason will need editing in two more places unless the describers are consolidated first.

title: UNATTRIBUTED_IMPORT and TERMINAL_DEAD_END name the same condition, split only by which file the developer touched
description:
downwind/blind_spots.py now carries two reasons for one fact about the import graph: a project file nothing was seen to import, which defines no test and which coverage attributed to no test.

downwind/rules.py:_blind_spot_reason reports it as UNATTRIBUTED_IMPORT when that file is the CHANGED one. _tests_downwind_of reports it as TERMINAL_DEAD_END when the same file is merely reached by the closure. So editing src/plugin.py and editing a helper src/plugin.py imports produce two different reason strings in .downwind.json and on the console for the identical blindness, and a developer reading the second has no way to tell it is the same problem they saw named differently last week.

The split is not meaningless -- the changed file is the thing they just edited, the reached file is a step removed -- but if that distinction is worth keeping it should be carried by the wording rather than by two enum members whose definitions are almost identical. Note the two rules also disagree slightly on their test: _blind_spot_reason checks only tests_in_module, _tests_downwind_of checks both relations.
design:
Either collapse to one reason and let the file field carry the difference, or keep both and rewrite the two docstrings so each states what the other is NOT. Do not leave them as they stand.

If collapsing, plugin.py:_describe_blind_spot renders reasons generically so it needs no change, but reports/downwind_suite.py writes the reason into .downwind.json, which is read back by the same tool version and so needs no migration.

Whichever way it goes, align the two conditions: there is no reason for one rule to consult tests_in_module alone while the other consults both.
acceptance_criteria: One reason covers the condition, or both remain with docstrings that make the boundary between them unambiguous. The condition each rule tests is spelled the same way in both places.

title: TERMINAL_DEAD_END may fire on a barren test package __init__.py
description:
so-n6b.29's dead-end rule refuses when the import closure terminates at an unattributed file yielding no tests by either relation. tests/__init__.py can be exactly that shape: pytest's importlib machinery may load it without the tracer seeing an edge, it defines no test, and under --cov=pkg coverage never measured it. Any source module imported by a test package's __init__.py would then refuse instead of selecting.

Unverified -- no profile of this repo was inspected while filing. The first step is to profile a project whose tests/ is a package and check whether tests/__init__.py lands in unattributed_modules with an empty tests_at_or_below.

Fails SAFE to the full suite and LOUDLY, naming the file, so it is not an MVP blocker under the downwind-mvp minimality rule. It is a precision problem: a project shaped this way would get a refusal for a large share of ordinary source edits, which is the difference between the tool being useful and not.
design: If it does fire, the natural fix mirrors the conftest fallback rather than the refusal: a test package's __init__.py governs the tests below it in exactly the way a conftest does, so tests_at_or_below(its directory) is an answer where a plugin has none. Weigh that against simply teaching the tracer to attribute pytest's own module loads, which would remove the dead end rather than paper over it.
acceptance_criteria: Either a profile of a package-shaped test tree shows tests/__init__.py does not become a terminal dead end, closing this as not-a-bug with the evidence recorded, or the fallback above lands with a unit test over a hand-built profile in that shape.

title: The project's own coverage under-reports every module its pytest11 plugin imports
description:
smoke-optimiser registers smoke_optimiser.plugin as a pytest11 entry point (pyproject.toml:44-45), so pytest imports that module -- and everything it imports -- before pytest-cov starts measuring. Those modules' import-time lines (imports, class bodies, def statements, module constants) are therefore never recorded as executed, and the coverage report shows them as misses even though every function in them is exercised.

Currently visible on:
* smoke_optimiser/downwind/blind_spots.py -- 40%, missing lines 13-52 and 62, which is the whole of BlindSpotReason, the BlindSpot field declarations and the in_report_order def line. Both functions are tested; only the statements that ran too early are missing.
* smoke_optimiser/reports/downwind_suite.py -- 44%, for the same reason via the same import chain.

The effect is a coverage figure that cannot be read at face value for these modules, which matters because the project uses per-module coverage as evidence when closing issues (so-jr5.1 was closed on '100% coverage on the module'). Nothing is actually untested here, but a reader cannot tell that from the number, and a genuine gap in one of these modules would hide among the artefact.

The usual remedy is COVERAGE_PROCESS_START plus coverage.process_startup(), or measuring under 'coverage run -m pytest' so measurement begins before plugin loading. Either is a change to how the project runs its own tests (Justfile, pyproject addopts), not to the library.
acceptance_criteria: A module imported by the pytest11 plugin reports coverage that reflects what the tests actually exercised, so a real gap in it is visible.

title: Derive precise test roots from what pytest actually collected, instead of falling back to the repository root
description:
A project that configures no testpaths and passes no path leaves pytest pointed
at the repository root, so the profile records a test root of '.' (smoke_optimiser/
profiler/scope.py). Because that root carries no information -- everything in the
tree is under it -- scope narrows there to the files pytest would collect by name:
test_*.py, *_test.py and conftest.py.

That keeps the profile usable, but it gives up a real signal. Test SUPPORT modules
-- tests/helpers/factories.py, a fixtures module, a package of builders -- match no
naming pattern, so under a repository-root scope a new one does not expire the
profile even though a regenerated profile would know about it (a test imports it,
so the import tracer records it). That is silent under-selection, the failure
so-n6b.1 exists to prevent, in the one configuration where the tool cannot see
enough to prevent it. Today the answer is a capture-time warning telling the user to
create tests/ and set testpaths.

The run itself knows better than its command line does. It collected specific test
files, and the import tracer saw which modules those files imported. The directories
containing the collected tests are a far more precise test root than '.', and are
observable from inside the profiled process where the scope is already resolved.
Recording those instead would restore the flat 'every .py file beneath the root'
rule for these projects, and let the warning become advice rather than a statement
about a narrower guarantee.

Design questions worth settling before implementing:

* Collected test files can be scattered (tests/, a package's own tests/ subdirectory,
  a doctest module at the root). Do their directories become several roots, or does a
  common ancestor? A common ancestor is often the repository root again, which buys
  nothing.
* A directory holding one collected test file is not necessarily all test code
  (a package with tests/ inside it also holds source). Coverage roots already claim
  the source, so overlap is probably harmless, but it should be a decision rather
  than an accident.
* This makes the scope depend on which tests were collected, so a run under -k or
  --ignore records a narrower scope than the project's real layout. so-n6b.24 is
  already about truncated runs being profiled as though complete; the same
  reasoning applies here and the two should agree.

title: Profiling appends its own --cov even when the project's addopts already set one
description:
runner.py:_build_pytest_command decides whether to add a coverage target by
inspecting config.pytest_args alone:

    has_cov_source = any(arg == "--cov" or arg.startswith("--cov=") for arg in args)
    if not has_cov_source:
        pytest_cmd.append(f"--cov={config.cov_source}")

pytest applies [tool.pytest.ini_options] addopts itself, inside the child
process, so a --cov living there is invisible here. When a project sets one --
this repository does, pyproject.toml:67 carries --cov=smoke_optimiser -- the
child receives BOTH the project's target and smoke-optimiser's appended one, and
pytest-cov's --cov is an appending option, so coverage measures the union.

Here the two happen to be the same string and nothing is observable. They need
not be: a project whose addopts say --cov=src/app, with no src/ package for
_discover_cov_target to find, gets --cov=src/app plus --cov=. and measures the
entire tree. The effects are a slower instrumented run, a total_branches
denominator covering code the project deliberately excluded from measurement,
and a recorded profile scope wider than the project asked for.

The fix is to decide the coverage target from what the child actually resolved
rather than from the parent's view of the command line -- the same reasoning
that put scope resolution inside the profiled process (smoke_optimiser/profiler/
scope.py). The hook can already see pytest-cov's resolved cov_source; the
question is whether the parent should stop appending and let the child's
configuration stand, or keep appending only when the child reports none.

Distinct from so-asl, which is about --cov-config replacing the project's
coverage configuration wholesale. This one is about the --cov flag on the
command line, and would remain after so-asl is fixed.

title: OutcomesFileModel doesn't enforce worker/worker_count co-nullability
description: OutcomesFileModel (smoke_optimiser/profiler/models.py:141) docstrings say worker and worker_count are each 'None when the run was serial', implying they're set or unset together, but nothing enforces that pairing -- a malformed outcomes file with worker set but worker_count None (or vice versa) would validate silently. Surfaced while fixing so-n6b.19, which added the equivalent model_validator pattern to BlindSpotModel/DownwindSuiteFile in downwind_suite.py. Lower confidence than that case: this is descriptive of expected writer behaviour rather than a hard invariant with a named failure mode, and no downstream code appears to assume the pairing -- worth a quick look to confirm it's worth enforcing before adding a model_validator.

title: The repro completeness test scrapes rendered --help text, so option names break it when Rich wraps them
description:
test_repro_command_completeness_against_help (tests/test_reports.py) checks that build_repro_command names every CLI option. It discovers the options by invoking --help and regexing the RENDERED output:

  all_options = re.findall(r"--([a-z-]+)", result.stdout)

That reads Rich's formatted help table, which is wrapped to the terminal width. An option name too long for the column is wrapped mid-name and scraped as a truncated one.

This is not hypothetical. Making the flags tri-state in so-qex renamed --allow-parallel-durations to the pair --allow-parallel-durations/--no-allow-parallel-durations, the line wrapped, and the test failed asserting that '--allow-parallel-du=' was missing from the repro command. It was patched by invoking help with env={"COLUMNS": "200"}, which works but only buys headroom -- a longer name, or a change to Rich's table layout, breaks it again the same way. The regex also cannot tell a real option from any other --token that appears in help text.

FIX: introspect the command instead of its rendering. typer.main.get_command(app) yields the click Command, whose .params carry each option's real names in .opts and .secondary_opts -- the negative half of a boolean pair lands in secondary_opts, which also removes the need for the test to strip a 'no-' prefix by hand. No terminal width involved, and no way for a formatting change to alter the answer.

Then drop the COLUMNS workaround and the comment explaining it.

The existing exclusion set (install-completion, show-completion, help, profile-only, optimise-only, smoke-file-path) still applies and should be kept as-is; note that with introspection the completion options come from click and may need matching on the same names.

title: cli_overrides is a stringly-keyed dict[str, Any], so a mistyped key silently does nothing
description:
resolve_config takes cli_overrides: dict[str, Any] (smoke_optimiser/config.py) and merges it by string key:

  for key, value in cli_overrides.items():
      if key in config_dict and value is not None:
          config_dict[key] = value

'if key in config_dict' means an override whose key does not match a FileConfig field is discarded without complaint. Nothing -- not ruff, not ty, not a test -- connects the dict literal built in cli.py's main to the field names it is supposed to address. Rename a FileConfig field, or typo a key at the call site, and the flag stops working while everything still passes.

This is the substrate that allowed so-qex. That bug was fixed by making boolean flags tri-state, which is correct, but it fixed one instance of a general weakness: the mapping from flag to config key is unchecked, and correctness depends on the author of each new flag getting an untyped dict entry right. so-jr5.4 adds a whole second command's worth of flags on top of it.

It also sits badly with GEMINI.md, which asks that functions not pass bare dicts around and that internal data be dataclasses.

DESIGN DECISION, hence opus:
  - A frozen dataclass of Optional fields mirroring FileConfig is the obvious shape, but it duplicates the field list in a third place (FileConfig, ResolvedConfig, and now this) and those three can still drift apart.
  - Alternatively derive the override container from FileConfig, or have resolve_config assert its keys are a subset of FileConfig.model_fields and fail loudly otherwise -- much smaller, catches typos at runtime on every invocation rather than at type-check time.
  - The mode keys (profile_only, optimise_only) are deliberately NOT FileConfig fields and are read by .get() before the merge loop, so any solution must keep them expressible without making them look like config keys.

Worth settling BEFORE so-jr5.4 wires up the downwind command's flags, since that is when the second batch of hand-written key strings gets added.

title: changed_files crashes with UnicodeDecodeError on a non-UTF-8 filename instead of raising GitStatusError
description:
smoke_optimiser/downwind/changes.py:_run_git_status runs 'git status --porcelain=v2 -z' via subprocess.run(text=True), which decodes stdout using the locale's preferred encoding (normally UTF-8). git itself places no encoding constraint on filenames on POSIX systems -- a path with non-UTF-8 bytes is legal and git handles it fine in -z/porcelain mode, which exists precisely to be byte-safe. text=True will raise UnicodeDecodeError for such a path, which is an unhandled exception rather than the module's own GitStatusError, breaking the contract that git/filesystem problems surface as GitStatusError.

Low real-world likelihood on this project (developer machines, normal source trees) but a clean fix: catch UnicodeDecodeError around the decode (or run capture_output with text=False and decode explicitly with errors='surrogateescape', a Python-standard byte-safe decoding), and raise GitStatusError with the path context.
acceptance_criteria: A test creates a file with a non-UTF-8 byte in its name (or simulates the decode failure) and asserts changed_files raises GitStatusError rather than UnicodeDecodeError.

title: Decide how changed_files should represent a path that is both staged-deleted and re-created untracked
description:
git status --porcelain=v2 can emit TWO records for the same path in one call: 'git rm --cached foo.py' followed by leaving the working file in place produces both a type-1 'D.' record (staged delete relative to HEAD) and a separate '?' untracked record for the same path, since the file no longer exists in the index. smoke_optimiser/downwind/changes.py:changed_files (built for so-7hr) parses each git-status record independently, so this case yields TWO ChangedFile entries for the same path -- ChangedFile('foo.py', DELETED) and ChangedFile('foo.py', ADDED) -- in the same frozenset[ChangedFile].

so-7hr's acceptance criteria only pin down uniqueness for renames ('a renamed file appears once, as its OLD path'); nothing says whether a path may appear more than once in the general case, and this is the one git-status shape where it can. Not a bug in so-7hr itself -- both records are individually correct descriptions of git's state -- but so-jr5.2 (the downwind rules) and so-jr5.4 (the command wiring both a changed_files call and its own existing_files enumeration) both need to know whether they may see two entries for one path, and if so, which kind should win when deciding blind spots. Left unhandled, a naive 'index changed_files by path' in a caller would silently drop one of the two entries depending on set/dict iteration order.

Reproduce: in a repo with a committed foo.py, run 'git rm --cached foo.py' (leaves the worktree file in place) and call changed_files(repo_root) -- the result contains both ChangedFile('foo.py', DELETED) and ChangedFile('foo.py', ADDED).
acceptance_criteria: A decision is recorded on whether changed_files should (a) keep emitting multiple entries per path in this case, documented as a caller obligation, or (b) collapse to a single entry with a defined precedence. Whichever is chosen, so-jr5.2 and/or so-jr5.4's descriptions are updated to state how they handle it, and a test pins the chosen behaviour.

title: Deduplicate _load_smoke_suite and _load_downwind_suite in plugin.py
description: smoke_optimiser/plugin.py's _load_smoke_suite and _load_downwind_suite (added for so-uom) are structurally identical: check the flag, resolve the path, exit if missing, try/except the same three ways (ValidationError/ValueError, blind Exception catch, version check against a SUPPORTED_*_VERSIONS set), differing only in which flag/option names, read_* function, and error-message noun ('smoke suite' vs 'downwind selection') they use. Extract a shared generic helper parameterised by flag name, file-path option name, reader callable, supported-versions set, and the noun used in messages, and have both thin wrappers call it. Purely mechanical -- no behavior change, existing tests in tests/test_plugin.py should pass unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: _load_smoke_suite and _load_downwind_suite share one implementation with no duplicated try/except/exit logic. All existing tests in tests/test_plugin.py pass unmodified.

title: Reconcile manual CHANGELOG.md breaking-change entries with release-please
description:
This project uses release-please (release-please-config.json, .release-please-manifest.json), which generates CHANGELOG.md from Conventional Commits -- specifically from a 'BREAKING CHANGE:' footer in the commit body, not from hand-written CHANGELOG prose.

so-n6b.16's implementation commit (7a16493, 'feat(profiler): version the profiling data file schema') added a manual '## Unreleased / ### BREAKING CHANGES' section to CHANGELOG.md by hand, because the acceptance criteria required the version bump to be noted as a breaking change. The commit message itself does not carry a 'BREAKING CHANGE:' trailer.

Risk: release-please manages CHANGELOG.md's release sections itself. A hand-written 'Unreleased' section may be clobbered or duplicated the next time release-please runs, and because the commit lacks the trailer, release-please will not classify the release as a major/breaking bump on its own -- the manual note and the tool's own record of the change can drift apart.

Fix is either: (a) confirm release-please preserves hand-written sections above its own generated ones and leave as-is, or (b) squash/reword history (or accept the drift once) so the next breaking-schema commit carries a proper 'BREAKING CHANGE:' footer instead of a hand-edited CHANGELOG section, and remove the manual section once release-please has picked it up. Low priority: cosmetic/process risk, not a functional bug.

title: Expire a profile when its recorded scope no longer covers what the next run would measure
description:
so-n6b.14 records the scope roots a profile was captured under, and so-n6b.1 expires a profile when an in-scope file is unknown to its maps. Neither notices when the SCOPE ITSELF changes. Widen --cov from smoke_optimiser to smoke_optimiser and scripts, and a whole tree becomes knowable that the maps have never seen: a regenerated profile would know it, the current one never will, and nothing expires. That is silent staleness of exactly the kind so-n6b.1 exists to prevent, arriving through configuration rather than through the tree.

THE HARD PART IS COMPUTING WHAT TO COMPARE AGAINST, and it is why this is not a one-line set comparison bolted onto so-n6b.1.

Deciding drift means knowing the scope the NEXT run would measure, ahead of running it. smoke-optimiser cannot currently determine that. runner.py:290-298 appends --cov={config.cov_source} only when config.pytest_args lacks a --cov, and nothing anywhere inspects the project's own [tool.pytest.ini_options] addopts -- pytest applies those itself, invisibly. This repository is the case in point: pyproject.toml:67 carries --cov=smoke_optimiser, and config.py's _discover_cov_target independently arrives at the same answer by a different route. On a project where those two disagree, a naive 'recorded != currently resolved' test is TRUE ON EVERY RUN AGAINST AN UNTOUCHED TREE -- the profile is born expired, every run takes the full-suite path, so-jr5.3 rewrites the profile, and the next run is expired again. That is precisely the failure so-n6b.14 was raised to eliminate, reintroduced through the comparison meant to strengthen it.

So this issue must first make the effective scope knowable ahead of a run -- by reading the project's pytest configuration the way pytest resolves it, or by probing (a collect-only run reporting the resolved --cov targets), or by another route that cannot disagree with what the profiling run will actually measure. Recording the scope is sound precisely because it observes the run; recomputing it must reach the same answer or it is worse than nothing.

SUBSET, NOT EQUALITY. Widening must expire: files become knowable that the maps have never seen. Narrowing must not: every file still in scope is one the maps already know, so the maps become a superset of what is asked of them, which is safe. Expiring on a narrowing costs one instrumented full run (so-jr5.3) for a configuration change that made the tool's job smaller. The test is 'the resolved scope is not a subset of the recorded scope', over normalised repo-relative roots by PREFIX -- smoke_optimiser/downwind is inside smoke_optimiser by prefix, not by string equality. Getting that backwards, and reading a widening as a narrowing, restores the silent staleness this issue exists to close.

COMPARE RESOLVED ROOTS, NEVER CONFIGURATION TEXT. Reordering flags, or adding an unrelated pytest option, must not expire a profile.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, do not re-propose:
• Compare recorded roots against config.cov_source union testpaths directly. This is the naive test above; it is unsound wherever the project's addopts carry a --cov, which is common and is true of this repository.
• Hash the addopts string. Expires on whitespace, flag order and unrelated options, and does not expire when the same scope is reached by a different route.
• Skip drift detection and rely on the tree comparison. That is so-n6b.1's MVP position and is safe but incomplete: a widened scope never expires, so the newly-in-scope tree stays permanently invisible.
acceptance_criteria: Widening the profiling scope expires the profile. Narrowing it does not, and the resulting selection for an in-scope changed file is unchanged -- a test for each. A project whose pytest addopts carry a --cov that differs from what config.py's _discover_cov_target returns is NOT expired on an untouched tree; this is the regression test that the naive comparison fails. The subset test is on normalised repo-relative roots by prefix, with a test distinguishing a prefix match from a string match. Reordering pytest flags does not expire a profile.
notes:
The soundness constraint is the whole issue. A drift check that can be permanently true is strictly worse than no drift check, because it pins the tool to the full-suite path forever while looking like it is working -- and so-jr5.3's instrumented fallback makes the loop self-sustaining and silent.

Covers the widening/narrowing asymmetry as well as the detection itself, so the correct semantics land in one piece rather than as a strict rule followed by a relaxation.

title: Repair an expired profile by running only the new test files, not the whole suite
description:
so-n6b.1 makes 'expired behaves exactly like absent: run the full suite', and so-jr5.3 runs that fallback instrumented so it rewrites the profile. That is the right MVP answer, and it is correct in every case. It is not always the CHEAPEST correct answer.

SCOPED DELIBERATELY TO ONE CASE: the only in-scope files unknown to the maps are new TEST files. Nothing else about the divergence -- no new source file, no new package. Adding a new source file keeps the full-suite fallback; there is no principled cheap repair there, because the new module is reached from existing files whose test attribution may have changed in ways only rerunning those tests can reveal.

In the new-test-file-only case the missing information is exactly what running those files produces. Running tests/test_discounts.py under instrumentation yields its coverage contexts, so the file -> tests map gains test_discounts against every file it executed, including the existing files it reaches transitively. That is the entry the stale profile was missing in so-n6b.1's own worked example -- a teammate's new test that exercises rates.py through discounts.py, invisible to a profile captured before it existed.

The import graph half is cheaper still. The tracer installs at pytest_configure specifically because project modules are imported during collection (runner.py:66-68), so a --collect-only pass rebuilds the whole graph without executing a single test. merge_graphs already exists in import_tracer.py.

WHAT MAKES IT HARDER THAN IT LOOKS, and why it is not part of the MVP:

• The merged profile is assembled from one tree state for most tests and another for the new ones, so ProfilingMeta.commit names only one of them. What the metadata MEANS after a partial merge needs deciding, not inheriting.
• _verify_contexts asserts the coverage contexts match the tests that ran. A partial run covers a fraction of the suite, so the check must distinguish 'partial by design' from the incomplete-data case so-jr5.3 exists to catch. Getting that wrong reintroduces exactly the silent partial-profile overwrite jr5.3's 'MUST NOT OVERWRITE A GOOD PROFILE WITH A PARTIAL ONE' guards against.
• unattributed_modules does not union cleanly: a module attributed in the full run may be unattributable in a partial one, because its importer was never loaded. Union grows the unattributed set, which is conservative (more refusals) rather than unsafe, but it means repeated partial repairs degrade the graph over time. Needs a bound.

GATED ON so-n6b.7. If new files arrive weekly the cliff is free and this is unnecessary complexity on the most safety-critical path in the tool. If they arrive daily -- and n6b.7 is being widened to report new TEST files separately, which is precisely this issue's population -- the saving is most of a suite most days. Do not start this before that distribution exists.
acceptance_criteria: An expired profile whose only unknown in-scope files are test files is repaired by running just those files under instrumentation, and the resulting selection matches what a full instrumented re-profile would have selected -- demonstrated by a test that constructs both and compares. Any other cause of expiry still takes the full-suite path. The merged profile's metadata states what it is, and a partial run that fails to produce complete data leaves the previous profile in place, per so-jr5.3. Repeated partial repairs do not monotonically grow unattributed_modules.
notes:
Scoped deliberately to the new-test-file case. Adding a new source file keeps the full-suite fallback: the new module is reached from existing files whose test attribution may have changed in ways only rerunning those tests can reveal, so there is no principled cheap repair.

This changes the RESPONSE to expiry, not the test for it. so-n6b.1's definition of expiry is untouched; what it supersedes is n6b.1's 'expired behaves exactly like absent', in this one case.

ALTERNATIVE CONSIDERED: repair from a --collect-only pass alone. That rebuilds the whole import graph for almost nothing, since the tracer installs at pytest_configure precisely because project modules are imported during collection. But it yields no coverage contexts, so the file -> tests map gains nothing -- and the file -> tests map is the half a new test file actually changes. The collect-only pass is worth doing as part of this, not instead of it.

title: Expire on a scope change only when the new scope is not a subset of the recorded one
description:
so-n6b.14 settled that a profile expires when its recorded scope roots differ from the ones the current configuration resolves to. For the MVP that is 'any difference', chosen for being one comparison with nothing to get wrong.

Any difference is stricter than necessary in one direction. WIDENING the scope must expire: new files become knowable, and a regenerated profile would know them, so the maps are stale in exactly so-n6b.1's sense. NARROWING cannot cause under-selection. If the scope goes from --cov=smoke_optimiser to --cov=smoke_optimiser/downwind, every file still in scope is one the maps already know -- the maps become a superset of what is asked of them, which is safe. Expiring there buys nothing and costs one instrumented full run (so-jr5.3), for a configuration change that made the tool's job smaller.

The refinement: expire when the current scope is not a subset of the recorded scope, rather than when the two differ.

Subset over roots, not over paths -- 'smoke_optimiser/downwind' is a subset of 'smoke_optimiser' by prefix, not by string equality, so the comparison is on normalised, repo-relative root paths with a prefix test. Getting that wrong in the unsafe direction (treating a widening as a narrowing) reintroduces the silent staleness so-n6b.14 exists to close, which is why it is a refinement rather than the MVP behaviour.
acceptance_criteria: Widening the profiling scope still expires the profile. Narrowing it does not, and the resulting selection is still correct -- demonstrated by a test that narrows the scope, asserts not-expired, and asserts the selection for an in-scope changed file is unchanged. The subset test is on normalised repo-relative root paths by prefix, with a test for the case that distinguishes a prefix match from a string match.
notes: Not blocking so-n6b.1: the MVP behaviour is correct, merely conservative. A narrowed scope costs one instrumented full run (so-jr5.3) for a configuration change that made the tool's job smaller, which is wasteful rather than wrong.

title: _tests_by_file silently drops a covered file that known_files does not contain
description:
Noticed while reading smoke_optimiser/downwind/maps.py during so-n6b.10.

_tests_by_file (maps.py:69) inverts every outcome's files_covered into 'covering', then returns a dict comprehension over known_files ONLY:

    return {path: frozenset(covering.get(path, ())) for path in known_files}

Any path a test actually executed that is absent from known_files is discarded without trace. known_files (maps.py:57) is measured_files | the graph's edge endpoints | unattributed_modules, so this rests on the unstated invariant that files_covered is a subset of measured_files for every outcome.

That invariant is plausible but not enforced anywhere, and there is at least one live reason to doubt it: so-746 records that the profile's paths are not yet repo-relative by construction, so files_covered and measured_files can be normalised differently and fail to match as strings even when they name the same file.

The consequence is not a wrong answer -- a dropped path is absent from known_files, so knows() is False, so jr5.2 refuses and runs the full suite. It fails in the safe direction. But it is silent: real coverage evidence we HELD is thrown away, and the resulting full-suite run is indistinguishable from a genuinely unknown file. In a component whose entire purpose is to make 'the map cannot answer' explicit rather than implicit, discarding an answer we had is worth making visible.

Fix is either to fold covering's keys into known_files (so a covered file is known by construction), or to assert the invariant and let a violation be loud. Which one depends on whether a covered-but-unmeasured file is considered possible at all -- so-746 may make the question moot by fixing the normalisation upstream.
acceptance_criteria: A file appearing in some outcome's files_covered but not in measured_files or the import graph is either folded into known_files or raises, rather than being silently dropped. Covered by a unit test over a hand-built profile with exactly that mismatch.

title: so-n6b.1's timezone acceptance criterion is a leak from the wall-clock expiry it rejected
description:
Noticed while settling so-n6b.10, which was the same class of defect: an acceptance criterion that contradicts its own issue's description.

so-n6b.1's description is emphatic that expiry is divergence and NOT age -- 'EXPIRY IS DIVERGENCE, NOT AGE ... it is a fact rather than a threshold: no configured number, no per-project tuning' -- and its ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED explicitly rejects 'Wall-clock age past a configured threshold', marked do-not-re-propose.

Its acceptance criteria nonetheless end with: 'Timezone-aware comparison wherever capture time is read.'

Under the divergence rule, capture time is never read. The test is a set comparison between the repository's current files and measured_files | the import graph's files; ProfilingMeta.timestamp plays no part. The criterion is a vestige of the rejected age-based design, and it is actively misleading: an implementer reading the acceptance criteria for a definition of done will look for a datetime comparison that should not exist, and may add one.

The project's timezone-awareness rule (GEMINI.md) is real and applies wherever datetimes ARE used -- ProfilingMeta.timestamp is one such place. But it is a global standing rule, not an acceptance criterion for this issue.

Fix: strike the sentence from so-n6b.1's acceptance criteria. No code change.
acceptance_criteria: so-n6b.1's acceptance criteria no longer reference capture time or timezone-aware comparison, and describe only the divergence test its description specifies.
close_reason:
Already satisfied. so-n6b.1's acceptance criteria no longer contain 'Timezone-aware comparison wherever capture time is read'; they were rewritten to the divergence test and end at 'An expired profile takes the full-suite path with expiry named as the reason.' No datetime comparison remains for an implementer to mistake for a definition of done.

The criteria do still say 'the scope roots recorded in the profile at capture time'. Read literally against this issue's acceptance wording that is a reference to capture time, but it is a scope reference -- which roots, as recorded when the profile was captured -- not a datetime comparison, and it is load-bearing for so-n6b.14. Confirmed as satisfying rather than violating the intent.

Closing this unblocks so-n6b.1, and through it the so-jr5.2 -> so-jr5.4 chain, which was the entire reason no P1 MVP work read as ready.

title: DownwindMaps.dependents_of does a fresh per-file graph walk instead of SCC-based memoization
description:
smoke_optimiser/downwind/maps.py's _closure() deliberately walks the dependents graph fresh for every file (O(V*(V+E)) worst case across the whole map) rather than memoizing per node, because naive per-node memoization can cache an incomplete closure computed mid-cycle. This is documented in the function's docstring as a correctness-over-performance tradeoff.

At the repo scales measured so far (smoke-optimiser ~35 files/91 edges, casey_ai/api 143 files, enphase_curtailer 271 files) this is fast (sub-millisecond to build the whole map). It could become a real cost on a much larger monorepo (thousands of files). The correct fix if it ever matters is Tarjan/Kosaraju SCC condensation: compute strongly-connected components once, closure each component as a unit (which also gets cycle self-inclusion for free), then propagate over the condensation DAG in reverse topological order -- rather than a fresh walk per node.

Not worth doing speculatively; filed so the tradeoff and its fix are recorded rather than rediscovered. Only act on this if profile-build time on a real project is measured to actually be a problem.
acceptance_criteria: Either closed as won't-fix with a measurement showing build time is fine at real project scale, or DownwindMaps._dependents_by_file is rewritten using SCC condensation with the same public behaviour and existing tests still passing.

title: Measure how often a new file appears, since that is what expires a profile
description:
A profile is expired once a file exists that its map has never seen, which is a
cliff: crossing it costs one instrumented full run, which rewrites the profile and
resets it.

Nobody has measured how often that is. If a working week of ordinary development
adds a file most days, the cliff is crossed most days and downwind selection is
worth much less than the median-37-of-2600 headline suggests. If it is crossed
weekly, it is free.

MEASURE, over the last few months of history in smoke-optimiser, casey_ai and
enphase_curtailer: for each commit, how many commits (and how much wall-clock time)
pass before a file appears that did not exist at that commit. Report the
distribution, not a mean -- the interesting number is how often the interval is
short enough to matter.

The result decides whether the divergence cliff needs softening, and if so it gives
a real distribution to design against instead of an invented threshold. It also
prices the alternative that was rejected on principle: a wall-clock expiry is only
worse than divergence if divergence is actually cheaper to live with.
acceptance_criteria:
A reported distribution of the interval between a commit and the next commit introducing a file it did not have, in commits and in wall-clock time, across all three repositories.

BROKEN DOWN BY, because the aggregate interval alone cannot price the alternatives:
• New TEST files separately from new SOURCE files. so-n6b.17 can repair the test-file case by running only those files, so the two populations have different costs and only the source-file interval prices the true cliff.
• Files IN SCOPE separately from files outside it, on the scope so-n6b.14 settled (the coverage targets union the pytest test paths). A new file outside that scope never expires anything, so counting it inflates the cliff rate.
• Files git TRACKS separately from untracked ones. so-n6b.14 settled that expiry enumerates tracked files only, on the basis that an untracked file is one you just created and so-7hr already puts it in the changed set. If the untracked population turns out to be large, that reasoning is worth rechecking against it.
notes: The breakdowns are not incidental. The aggregate interval cannot distinguish the case so-n6b.17 can repair cheaply (new test files) from the one that stays expensive (new source files), and under so-n6b.14's scope some new files never expire a profile at all. Asking for the splits up front costs the measurement script almost nothing; retrofitting them means running the history again.

title: ProfilingData uses two words for one concept: unattributable_branches but unattributed_modules
description:
ProfilingData carries unattributable_branches (added by an earlier issue) and ImportGraph carries unattributed_modules (added by so-aeo). They name the same idea -- something the profile observed but could not tie to a test -- with two different words, in adjacent fields of the same dataclass tree.

The existing convention across the codebase is 'unattributable': coverage_db.py
uses it for the local variable, the frozen dataclass field and the comment
explaining the summarised context list. so-aeo introduced 'unattributed' without
noticing, so the new field is the odd one out and should be the one to change.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/profiler/models.py (ImportGraph field and docstring,
ImportGraphModel field), smoke_optimiser/profiler/import_tracer.py (snapshot,
merge_graphs, write_graph, module docstring), smoke_optimiser/cli.py
(_save_profiling_data), tests/test_import_tracer.py and
tests/test_profiler_models.py.

Note this is a profile format change: the field name appears in the JSON, so an
existing .smoke_profiling_data.json fails validation afterwards and must be
regenerated. That is the established behaviour for this file (see so-d8v and
so-aeo, which both made new fields required for the same reason), but it is worth
doing before so-jr5.2 starts reading the field rather than after.

Too small to be urgent, too easy to fix later to leave undecided.

title: Measure the import tracer's overhead on a large suite
description:
so-aeo added an ImportTracer that replaces builtins.__import__ and importlib.import_module for the whole profiling run. Every execution of every import statement in the suite now goes through a Python-level wrapper that resolves the target name, walks its ancestors and updates a set.

The cost is UNMEASURED. On smoke-optimiser itself the suite is far too small and
too fast for the difference to be distinguishable from noise, so nothing here
tells us what it does to a real suite.

This matters because so-jr5.3's whole argument for regenerating the profile in the
background rests on profiling being cheap: it quotes a measured +11% for coverage
instrumentation on enphase_curtailer (61s -> 68s with --cov-context=test). If the
tracer adds materially to that, the trade-off changes, and the capture may need to
become optional rather than always-on.

WHAT TO DO. Profile a large suite (enphase_curtailer, 2600 tests, or casey_ai/api,
1389 tests) three ways -- plain, with coverage instrumentation only, and with
instrumentation plus the tracer -- and record the deltas. The comparison needs the
tracer to be switchable to run at all, which is itself a useful outcome: today it
installs unconditionally from the profiling hook.

If the overhead is small, record the number next to the +11% in so-n6b and close
this. If it is not, file the follow-up to make capture optional.

title: The canonical repro command emitted --no-allow-ordered, which the CLI rejects
description:
build_repro_command emitted '--no-allow-ordered' when allow_ordered was off, but --allow-ordered is declared as a bare flag with no negative form. Pasting the 'Repro:' line printed in the summary therefore failed with 'No such option: --no-allow-ordered' -- the one command whose entire job is to reproduce the run did not run.

Verified before the fix:
  $ uv run smoke-optimiser --no-allow-ordered --optimise-only
  Error: No such option: --no-allow-ordered  Did you mean --allow-ordered?

FIXED while implementing so-u3i, since that issue added a second boolean flag and copying the broken shape was not an option. Boolean flags are now emitted only in their positive form and omitted when off. tests/test_reports.py asserts the absent case explicitly, and the completeness test now turns every boolean on so each must be named.

Filed after the fact so the history exists.
close_reason: Fixed as part of so-u3i; boolean flags now emit only their positive form and tests cover both the present and absent cases.

title: Ingest assumes every measured file is Python, so honouring a project's coverage plugins would crash on template files
description:
read_coverage_db in smoke_optimiser/profiler/coverage_db.py builds a PythonFileReporter for every row in the coverage database's file table:

    reporter = PythonFileReporter(absolute_path, cov)

coverage.py supports file-type plugins (django_coverage_plugin, mako, jinja) which put NON-Python files into that same table and supply their own FileReporter implementation. Asking PythonFileReporter to parse a .html template will fail, and the failure lands in a code path whose stated stance is that every error is fatal -- so profiling would abort outright on any project using one of these plugins.

LATENT TODAY, REACHABLE THE MOMENT so-asl LANDS. runner.py currently replaces the project's coverage configuration with a minimal rcfile containing only 'branch = True', which discards any configured plugins along with everything else. So the file table is Python-only by accident. so-asl exists precisely to stop discarding the project's config; the moment it does, plugin-registered files start appearing and this crashes. The two must land together.

The correct fix is to ask coverage for the right reporter rather than hard-coding one -- coverage's own reporting layer resolves a FileReporter per file via its plugin registry. Whether non-Python files should then contribute branches to the map at all is a design question worth deciding explicitly rather than falling out of the implementation: a template's 'branches' may not be a meaningful selection signal.
acceptance_criteria: A coverage database containing a file registered by a coverage file-type plugin is ingested without error, and the decision about whether such files contribute branches is documented rather than incidental.

title: Profile JSON is written in non-deterministic order, so two identical profiling runs produce byte-different files
description:
_save_profiling_data in smoke_optimiser/cli.py serialises every frozenset with bare list(), which takes Python's set iteration order:

    branches_covered=list(po.branches_covered)
    files_covered=list(po.files_covered)
    markers=list(po.markers)
    total_branches=list(profiling_data.total_branches)
    measured_files=list(profiling_data.measured_files)
    unattributable_branches=list(profiling_data.unattributable_branches)

Set ordering varies with insertion history and string hashing, so profiling the same tree twice yields JSON that differs everywhere despite describing identical data. That makes profiles impossible to diff, impossible to check into a repository usefully, and hides real changes in the noise -- which matters as soon as anyone wants to see what a code change did to the coverage map.

Sorting is the obvious fix. Note it is six lines, all in one function, which is why this is filed rather than fixed inline. Consider whether sorting belongs in the model layer instead, so anything else that serialises a profile inherits it.

Sizes are modest -- this repository has a few hundred branches, enphase_curtailer's 2600-test suite would be in the low tens of thousands -- so the sort cost is not a concern at realistic scale.
acceptance_criteria: Profiling the same tree twice with no source changes produces byte-identical JSON, ignoring the meta block's timestamp and command.

title: Parallel pytest workers (xdist) would race on the single shared outcomes JSON file
design:
DECIDED 2026-09-06 (user): SUPPORT xdist, do not reject it.

RATIONALE. Half this tool is the coverage map, half is the time-based suite
construction. Wanting only the map is a completely normal use (so-jr5's
change-based selection consumes the map and never reads a duration). Parallel
profiling is fine for that half, so it must not warn loudly at profile time.
Contended durations only matter to the half that uses time, so that is the
half that objects.

CAPTURE. Per-worker outcomes files keyed by PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER, merged by the
runner after the run (union across files). Detection must be RUNTIME, not
arg-string sniffing: xdist can be switched on by the target project's own
pytest.ini addopts, never appearing in --pytest-args, which is the exact
silent-data-loss case this issue is about. The plugin reads PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER
and PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER_COUNT from its own process.

RECORD. The worker count lands in the profile (ProfilingMeta), so the fact
travels with the artefact rather than living in stderr.

CONSUME. The time-based optimiser ERRORS on a profile recorded with >1 worker,
with an explicit override flag to proceed. A coverage-per-second ranking built
on contended timings is confidently wrong and looks fine, so a warning is not
enough. The map-only consumers stay silent.
close_reason: xdist supported: per-worker outcomes files merged by the runner, worker count recorded in the profile, time-based optimiser errors on a parallel profile with an --allow-parallel-durations override. Verified end to end with real pytest-xdist: 93/93 tests captured across 2 workers.

title: check_prerequisites looks for pytest on PATH but the runner invokes it as a module
description:
check_prerequisites gates on pytest being an executable on PATH:

    if shutil.which('pytest') is None:
        raise RuntimeError('pytest not found in PATH')

but every actual invocation runs it as a module of the current interpreter:

    pytest_cmd = [sys.executable, '-m', 'pytest', ...]

The two can disagree in both directions.

FALSE NEGATIVE (the common one): pytest is importable by sys.executable but not
on PATH. This is normal when smoke-optimiser is invoked via 'uv run', via
'python -m', from a virtualenv whose bin directory is not on PATH, or from a
tox/nox session. Profiling is refused even though it would work.

FALSE POSITIVE: a pytest on PATH belonging to a DIFFERENT environment satisfies
the check while sys.executable has no pytest, so the check passes and the
subprocess then fails with 'No module named pytest'.

FIX: test what is actually used -- importlib.util.find_spec('pytest') against
the running interpreter -- and say which interpreter was checked when it fails.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py:58

NOTE: tests/test_runner.py::test_check_prerequisites_success patches
shutil.which, so the patch target moves with the fix.

ACCEPTANCE: profiling proceeds in an environment where pytest is importable but
absent from PATH.

title: Line-level downwind selection, with git-aware remapping of shifted line numbers
description:
so-n6b deliberately ships FILE-level downwind selection: a changed file
selects every test that has ever executed any line in it. This is the follow-up
that narrows it to the lines actually touched.

WHY IT WAS NOT DONE FIRST. Line numbers shift. Insert one line at the top of a
file and every line number below it moves, so a line-level map silently
mismatches after almost any edit -- and silent mismatch means silent
under-selection, the one failure mode this feature must never have. File-level
is immune to line shifts, reformatting, and refactors within a file.

WHAT THIS NEEDS. Git-aware remapping: track how lines moved between the commit
the profile was taken at (ProfilingMeta.commit is already recorded) and HEAD, so
a profiled line number still resolves to the right line today. `git diff -U0`
between those two commits gives the hunks to translate through.

DO NOT START THIS UNTIL file-level has been measured in real use. On enphase the
file-level map has a median of 37 tests per file out of 2600 -- if that is
already fast enough, the extra precision buys nothing and costs a whole
remapping layer that can be subtly wrong.

title: downwind --src accepts a value that a --cov in --pytest-args silently overrides
description:
so-jr5.3 added --src to the downwind command, so the message refusing an undiscovered coverage source can offer a command the user can paste back. The smoke command rejects --src alongside a --cov in --pytest-args as a conflict it cannot honour (cli.py, _validate_option_combinations). downwind has no such check.

Passing both to downwind is therefore accepted and one of them quietly does nothing: check_prerequisites returns early when supplies_cov_source(config.pytest_args) is true, so the --src the user just typed never reaches the command line. Harmless to the profile, which is measured under the --cov they gave, but it means the tool accepts a contradiction and acts on half of it -- and the two commands disagree about whether the same pair of options is an error.

Where: smoke_optimiser/cli.py. _validate_option_combinations is shaped around the smoke command arguments and would need the relevant half extracted, or downwind given its own check.

Note the two commands read different args keys: smoke checks its own --pytest-args, downwind profiling run uses the PROFILING pytest_args rather than downwind_pytest_args, so the check must look at the same string check_prerequisites does or it will disagree with it.
acceptance_criteria: Passing --src to downwind alongside a --cov in the arguments the fallback profiles under is rejected with the same reasoning smoke uses, rather than silently ignoring one of them.

title: Three near-identical helpers read back the per-worker files the profiling hook writes
description:
runner.py now has three functions doing the same four steps: glob the per-worker siblings of a base path, read each, unlink each, and merge the results.

  _read_iteration_outcomes  -> OutcomesFileModel, merged by dict update
  _read_iteration_graph     -> read_graph, merged by merge_graphs
  _read_iteration_read_map  -> read_read_map, merged by merge_read_maps

The glob pattern (stem + '*' + suffix) and the unlink loop are copied verbatim between them, and each of the three merges resolves what one worker could not attribute against what the others could. HookArtefacts already groups the three paths, so the shape is half recognised.

The pattern is what makes xdist correct -- a shared file would be overwritten by whichever worker finished last, silently losing most of the suite -- so it is worth having in one place with that reasoning stated once, rather than three times with the risk of a fourth reader-writer pair getting it subtly wrong.

Low priority: the duplication is stable and each copy is correct today. File so the next addition consolidates rather than copying again.
